Module 8

Memory and configuration in practice

Module 2 looked at memory from inside the kernel: the MS-DOS arena of memory control blocks and FreeBSD's vm_map. This module looks at the whole machine, from the administrator's chair. How is the memory of a running system laid out, who uses it, and how do you find out? What does one line of CONFIG.SYS cost, and what does one line of rc.conf do? On MS-DOS 4.00 every answer is measured on the system built from source: we map the first megabyte, price every CONFIG.SYS keyword in bytes, load the 1988 EMM386.SYS and talk to it through INT 67h, and watch the Microsoft C 5.10 heap run out. On FreeBSD 15.1 we read the real configuration files of the release, run the rcorder algorithm by hand, write an rc.d script, and run memory experiments in the course's virtual machine. The two systems answer the same questions in opposite ways: one was designed around memory that was always too small, the other around memory that is never what it seems.

MS-DOS 2d04cacFreeBSD release/15.1.027 source listings2 study cases6 exercisesabout 125 min read
Francesco Valerio Buccoli · francesco@buccoli.com

Learning goals. After this module you can:

  • Draw the PC memory map as MS-DOS 4.00 sees it (conventional memory, upper memory area, HMA, extended and expanded memory) and locate each region on a running system with MEM, DEBUG and a small program.
  • Account for every byte of conventional memory that a CONFIG.SYS line costs, from the structure sizes in the source (BUFFINFO, SFT entries, CDS entries, stacks, device drivers).
  • Explain how EMM386.SYS emulates an expanded memory board with the 386's paging and virtual-8086 mode, and use INT 67h from your own program to allocate and map pages.
  • Compare the MS-DOS C heap (near and far heaps of Microsoft C 5.10 over INT 21h function 48h) with FreeBSD's malloc (jemalloc over mmap), and predict what each reports when memory runs out.
  • Read FreeBSD's memory statistics (sysctl vm.stats.vm, vmstat, top, swapinfo) and relate each number to a page queue in sys/vm.
  • Trace FreeBSD's boot-time configuration from loader.conf through /etc/rc, rc.conf and rcorder to the rc.d scripts, and write a working rc.d script that follows the rc.subr conventions.
  • Map each MS-DOS configuration mechanism to its FreeBSD counterpart, and say for each setting whether it takes effect at boot, at run time, or on the next service start.
  • Evaluate the cost of a configuration mistake on each system.

Prerequisites.

  • Module 0 (the lab, tools/dos_run.py, tools/dos_tools.py), Module 1 (SYSINIT and CONFIG.SYS, Section 1.5; the FreeBSD loader, Section 1.4), Module 2 (the arena, Section 2.5; Study case 2.C), Module 3 (COMMAND.COM, AUTOEXEC.BAT and the environment, Sections 3.6 and 3.7).
  • Some 8086 assembly (Module 1) and C. For FreeBSD: a shell, and the virtual machine for the runtime parts.

8.1 The PC memory map under MS-DOS 4.00#

Five kinds of memory#

Real mode forms 20-bit addresses (Module 1, Section 1.1), so the 8086 can address 1 MB. IBM's PC design gave the first 640 KB to RAM and reserved the 384 KB above it for the adapters: video memory and the ROMs of the video card, the disk controller and the system BIOS. Everything that came later had to fit around that decision. By 1988 a PC could have five kinds of memory:

Kind Addresses Reached by Who uses it in MS-DOS 4.00
Conventional 0 to 640 KB (00000-9FFFF) any real-mode program DOS, drivers, COMMAND.COM, programs: everything in the arena
Upper memory area (UMA) 640 KB to 1 MB (A0000-FFFFF) any real-mode program video memory, adapter ROMs, BIOS; free gaps for an EMS page frame
High memory area (HMA) first 64 KB above 1 MB minus 16 bytes (100000-10FFEF) real mode, FFFF:0010-FFFF:FFFF, only with the A20 line enabled nobody (see below)
Extended memory above 1 MB, up to 16 MB on a 286 protected mode, or the BIOS block move (INT 15h function 87h) RAMDRIVE /E, SMARTDRV, VDISK, and EMM386's pool
Expanded memory (EMS) not in the address space: pages on a board, or in extended memory INT 67h, through a 64 KB page frame in the UMA RAMDRIVE /A, BUFFERS=/X, applications

The first megabyte is the only memory that MS-DOS 4.00 manages. Its arena (Module 2, Section 2.5) starts just above the kernel and ends at the top of conventional memory, which SYSINIT takes from INT 12h (Module 1). Everything else is used by device drivers, each with its own scheme, as this section shows.

Extended memory and the INT 15h convention#

The 80286 and 80386 can address 16 MB and 4 GB, but only in protected mode. The PC/AT BIOS offered two services for real-mode software: INT 15h function 88h returns the number of KB above 1 MB, and function 87h copies a block between any two physical addresses by switching to protected mode and back. MS-DOS 4.00 asks for the size once, during SYSINIT, and stores it in the SYSINITVAR structure that function 52h returns (Module 2):

MS-DOS 4.00Listing 8.1 – SYSINIT records the extended memory size at boot (SYSINIT1.ASM lines 535-539)Source ↗
        mov     ah,88h
        int     15h                             ;check extended memory size
        jc      No_Ext_Memory
        mov     es:[di].SYSI_EXT_MEM,ax         ;save extended memory size
No_Ext_Memory:

SYSI_EXT_MEM is the last field of the structure (SYSVAR.INC line 28). DOS itself never uses it; MEM prints it as "total extended memory" and then calls function 88h again for "available extended memory" (MEM.C lines 770-790). The two numbers differ because of a convention, not an allocator. A driver that wants extended memory hooks INT 15h and makes function 88h report less: the memory above the new, lower limit is now the driver's. RAMDRIVE.SYS does exactly that:

MS-DOS 4.00Listing 8.2 – RAMDRIVE answers INT 15h function 88h itself (RAMDRIVE.ASM lines 2013-2033)Source ↗
;
;       This piece of code determines the size of extended memory
;       which was allocated before this driver and then subtracts
;       the amount it has allocated for itself
;
;       inputs: ah = 88h is of interest
;       outputs: ax = size of extended memory allocated by all before and
;                including us
;       regs used: flags
;
        pushf
        cmp     ah,88h
        je      mem_det
        popf
        jmp     [old_15]
mem_det:
        mov     ax,[int15_size]
        popf
        clc
        sti
        iret

Each driver takes memory from the top and lowers the limit, so the drivers stack up downwards from 16 MB. Nothing records who owns what; a driver that ignores the convention (the older VDISK.SYS allocated from the bottom, at 1 MB, and marked its memory with a header there) collides with the others. EMM386's allocator says it plainly: "We do not care for compatibility with vdisk" (ALLOCMEM.ASM lines 165-171). How does a real-mode driver copy data above 1 MB? RAMDRIVE has four configurations (lines 197-221); for /E on a 286 it uses LOADALL, an undocumented 286 instruction that loads every register, including the hidden base of a segment register, from a table at 0080:0000, so that one segment can point above 1 MB while the CPU stays in real mode (lines 896-925; the instruction is emitted as raw bytes, DW 050FH, at line 1113). The comment's "WARNING NUMBER ONE" is a fair summary of the era: the trick works only where a non-maskable interrupt halts the machine anyway.

The HMA, A20, and what MS-DOS 4.00 does not have#

On the 8086, FFFF:0010 wraps around to linear 00000. On a 286 or later it addresses 100000, the first byte above 1 MB, so real-mode code can reach almost 64 KB above 1 MB: the high memory area. For compatibility with programs that relied on the wrap-around, the AT added a gate on address line 20 (A20), controlled through the keyboard controller; with the gate closed, the wrap-around comes back. MS-DOS 5.0 later shipped HIMEM.SYS, an XMS (eXtended Memory Specification) driver that manages A20, the HMA and extended memory, and the DOS=HIGH and DEVICEHIGH= keywords that move DOS and drivers out of conventional memory. None of this exists in 4.00. A search of v4.0/src shows:

  • no file named HIMEM* and no occurrence of XMS in any .ASM, .INC, .C or .H file;
  • no DOS, HIGH or DEVICEHIGH keyword in the CONFIG.SYS table (Listing 1.22 in Module 1), and no upper-memory link in function 58h, which only sets the allocation strategy (Module 2, Section 2.5);
  • the word "himem" only in MEMM, where it means two other things: "the himem area (just below 16M)", an OEM-specific memory pool that the shipped build disables with -DNOHIMEM (MEMM/MEMM/MAKEFILE lines 51-54), and "the EMS 4.1 standard himem at 1M", the 64 KB that EMM386 leaves free at 1 MB (ALLOCMEM.ASM lines 401-425); INDEXMA.ASM has an unrelated HIMEM EQU;
  • A20 code only inside drivers that must open the gate for their own use: RAMDRIVE.ASM, SMARTDRV.ASM, IBM's 386 XMA emulator (DEV/XMAEM/INDEINI.ASM, through port 92h) and EMM386 (MEMM/MEMM/A20TRAP.ASM and several of its neighbours).

So in MS-DOS 4.00 the HMA is unused, A20 is left as the BIOS set it (Lab 8.1 finds it disabled in our emulator), and every byte of DOS, every driver and every TSR lives below 640 KB.

Expanded memory: bank switching#

Expanded memory solved a different problem: the 8088 PC and XT had no memory above 1 MB at all. The Lotus/Intel/Microsoft Expanded Memory Specification (LIM EMS) puts memory on an adapter board and makes it visible through a 64 KB page frame in a free part of the UMA, divided into four 16 KB windows. A program asks the expanded memory manager (EMM, a device driver) for logical pages of 16 KB, receives a handle, and asks the EMM to map a logical page into a window. The board then routes accesses to that window to the chosen page of its own memory. This is bank switching: the address space stays at 1 MB, and the program chooses which 64 KB of a much larger memory it can see.

The interface is INT 67h with the function in AH, much like INT 21h. The functions this module uses:

AH Function Returns
40h Get status AH = 0 if the manager works
41h Get page frame address BX = segment of the page frame
42h Get unallocated page count BX = free pages, DX = total pages
43h Allocate pages (BX = count) DX = handle
44h Map page (AL = window, BX = logical page, DX = handle) AH = status
45h Deallocate pages (DX = handle) AH = status
46h Get version AL = version in BCD, 40h for 4.0
53h, 58h EMS 4.0: handle names; mappable physical address array

A program finds out whether a manager is present by looking at the device driver behind the INT 67h vector: its name field, at offset 0Ah of the segment, must read EMMXXXX0. MEM instead checks that the vector is not zero and that functions 40h and 46h succeed (MEM.C lines 832-869). Section 8.3 shows how EMM386.SYS provides the same interface without any board.

8.2 Measuring memory on MS-DOS#

What MEM reports, and how#

MEM is new in 4.00. It is a C program (Microsoft C, with the message services of the 4.00 tree) with three levels of detail: no switch, /PROGRAM and /DEBUG, which set DataLevel to 0, 1 and 2 (MEM.C lines 304-309). With the lab image's CONFIG.SYS (FILES=20, BUFFERS=20, DEVICE=\ANSI.SYS), /PROGRAM prints:

Terminal
$ python tools/dos_run.py "MEM /PROGRAM"
Output 8.1 – MEM /PROGRAM on MS-DOS 4.00 built from source, lab image
  Address     Name          Size       Type
  ───────     ────────     ──────     ──────
  000000                   000400     Interrupt Vector
  000400                   000100     ROM Communication Area
  000500                   000200     DOS Communication Area

  000700      IO           002510     System Program

  002C10      MSDOS        008E00     System Program

  00BA10      IO           004E90     System Data
                ANSI       001180      DEVICE=
                           000380      FILES=
                           000100      FCBS=
                           0029A0      BUFFERS=
                           0001C0      LASTDRIVE=
                           000CD0      STACKS=
  0108B0      COMMAND      001640     Program
  011F00      COMMAND      000030     Data
  011F40      COMMAND      0000A0     Environment
  011FF0      MEM          000030     Environment
  012030      MEM          012F00     Program
  024F40      MSDOS        07B0B0     -- Free --


    655360 bytes total memory
    655360 bytes available
    581568 largest executable program size

  15728640 bytes total extended memory
  15728640 bytes available extended memory

All numbers are hexadecimal except the totals. The first three lines are not measured at all: MEM prints the constants 0/400h, 400h/100h and 500h/200h (MEM.C lines 382-410). IO runs from 0700h to the segment of SYSINITVAR (function 52h), and MSDOS from there to the first memory control block (MCB). From 00BA10 on, every line is one block of the arena, walked exactly as in Study case 2.C: the address column is the MCB's address, the size excludes the 16-byte MCB. MSDOS ... -- Free -- is the last, free block (owner 0); the name MSDOS is just what MEM prints for free memory.

The interesting block is the one owned by 8, "System Data": everything SYSINIT allocated while it processed CONFIG.SYS. MEM can break it down because SYSINIT writes a small header, a DEVMARK, in front of every table it builds:

MS-DOS 4.00Listing 8.3 – A DEVMARK has the layout of an MCB, with a letter instead of 'M' or 'Z' (DEVMARK.INC lines 3-19)Source ↗
DEVMARK struc
DEVMARK_ID        db      0
DEVMARK_SEG       dw      0
DEVMARK_SIZE      dw      0
DEVMARK_DUM       db      3 dup (?)
DEVMARK_FILENAME  db      8 dup (' ')
DEVMARK ends

DEVMARK_STK     equ     'S'
DEVMARK_DEVICE  equ     'D'
DEVMARK_IFS     equ     'I'
DEVMARK_BUF     equ     'B'
DEVMARK_CDS     equ     'L' ;lastdrive
DEVMARK_FILES   equ     'F'
DEVMARK_FCBS    equ     'X'
DEVMARK_INST    equ     'T' ;used for SYSINIT BASE for INSTALL= command.
DEVMARK_EMS_STUB equ    'E'

SetDevMark writes one at the current allocation point and advances it by one paragraph (SYSINIT1.ASM lines 2577-2601), and MEM walks these sub-blocks inside the owner-8 block with the same segment + size + 1 rule as the arena, translating the letters into DEVICE=, FILES= and so on (MEM.C lines 488-553). A second arena inside the first one: the 16-byte header is why each CONFIG.SYS table costs 16 bytes more than its size column. Check it on Output 8.1: the six sub-blocks add up to 4E30h bytes, plus 6 x 10h for the DEVMARKs, gives exactly the 4E90h of the System Data block.

"Largest executable program size"#

The summary line most people read is computed from MEM's own process:

MS-DOS 4.00Listing 8.4 – MEM measures the block it was loaded into (MEM.C line 687)Source ↗
        free_mem = (DOS_TopOfMemory * 16l) - (FP_SEG(PSPptr)*16l);                                                               /* ;an000;ac005; */

DOS_TopOfMemory is the word at offset 2 of the program segment prefix (PSP), the first segment after the block DOS gave the program; the PSP segment is where the block starts. EXEC loads a program into the largest free block (Module 2, Section 2.6), so the difference is the largest block that existed when MEM started, the size of the biggest program you could run next. Output 8.1 confirms it: MEM's block (12F00h) plus its MCB plus the free block (7B0B0h) is 8DFC0h = 581,568 bytes. MEM had already given back most of its block before it printed anything; the C start-up code does that (Section 8.5). CHKDSK computes the same quantity from its own PSP (CHKDSK2.ASM lines 356-362), and Output 0.1 in Module 0 shows it 16 bytes lower: 581,552. Why? Lab 8.1 answers it.

What each CONFIG.SYS line costs#

Module 1 measured one data point (BUFFERS=30, FILES=40). Lab 8.2 boots the system once per variant and builds the full price list; the result, with the structure sizes that explain it, is the table below. The baseline is a boot without CONFIG.SYS (589,424 bytes), where the defaults apply: FILES=8, FCBS=4, 15 buffers on a machine with more than 512 KB, STACKS=9,128 on an AT-class machine, and drives up to E: (SYSINIT1.ASM lines 1142-1161, lines 1434-1446).

Line Largest program Cost Where the bytes go
(none) 589,424 0
BUFFERS=1 596,864 -7,440 14 fewer buffers of 20 + 512 bytes
BUFFERS=30 581,440 7,984 15 more buffers (7,980) and a second hash bucket (8, rounded)
FILES=40 587,536 1,888 32 more SFT entries of 59 bytes
FCBS=16,8 588,720 704 12 more FCB-SFT entries of 59 bytes, rounded to paragraphs
STACKS=0,0 592,720 -3,296 no stack code (2,048), no 9 x (8 + 128) stacks, no DEVMARK
STACKS=18,256 585,904 3,520 18 x (8 + 256) = 4,752 instead of 1,232 bytes
LASTDRIVE=Z 587,584 1,840 26 instead of 5 current-directory structures of 88 bytes
DEVICE=\ANSI.SYS 584,928 4,496 the driver's resident part, 4,480 bytes
DEVICE=\RAMDRIVE.SYS 64 522,112 67,312 the disk itself (64 KB) inside the driver
DEVICE=\RAMDRIVE.SYS 64 /E 587,408 2,016 resident code only; 64 KB of extended memory
DEVICE=\SMARTDRV.SYS 256 589,424 0 not installed: "No hard drives on system"
INSTALL=\KEYB.COM IT,,\KEYBOARD.SYS 583,568 5,856 the TSR (5,776) and a 48-byte hole
DEVICE=\EMM386.SYS 551,936 37,488 the 386 monitor's resident part (Section 8.3)
EMM386 + BUFFERS=50 /X 559,904 29,520 60 buffers (two EMS pages of 30) in expanded memory, 32 bytes below 640 KB

The table is built from paragraph-exact MEM output (Lab 8.2 keeps it) and the structure definitions:

  • A disk buffer is a 20-byte BUFFINFO header plus a sector (BUFFER.INC lines 9-31). 4.00 organises buffers in hash buckets of up to 15, each with an 8-byte BUFFER_HASH_ENTRY (lines 64-72), and rounds the hash table and the buffer area separately to paragraphs: 15 buffers take 16 + 7,984 = 8,000 bytes (1F40h in MEM), one buffer 16 + 544 = 560 (230h).
  • An SFT entry (the FILES= table, Module 2, Section 2.3) is 59 bytes. The first five are inside MSDOS.SYS; the FILES= block holds the rest after a 6-byte link and count, so FILES=8 costs 6 + 3 x 59, rounded to 192 bytes (0C0h). FCBS= uses the same entry format.
  • LASTDRIVE= allocates one current directory structure (CDS, curdir_list, 88 bytes: CURDIR.INC lines 18-29) per drive letter: 5 x 88 = 440, rounded to 448 (1C0h); 26 x 88 = 2,288 (8F0h).
  • STACKS= copies the stack-switching interrupt code (the first 2,048 bytes of SYSINIT, up to Endstackcode) and adds STACK_COUNT x (EntrySize + STACK_SIZE), with EntrySize = 8:
MS-DOS 4.00Listing 8.5 – The STACKS= space formula (SYSINIT1.ASM lines 1478-1484)Source ↗
;       Space for Internal Stack area = STACK_COUNT(ENTRYSIZE + STACK_SIZE)
        MOV     AX, EntrySize
        ADD     AX, [STACK_SIZE]
        MOV     CX, [STACK_COUNT]
        MUL     CX
        call    ParaRound                       ; Convert size to pargraphs
        ADD     [MEMHI], AX

Three entries need more than arithmetic. SMARTDRV.SYS caches hard disks only: it asks INT 13h function 08h about drive 80h and gives up with the message we captured when there is none (SMARTDRV.ASM lines 5651-5673), and our lab machine has only a floppy. KEYB costs more than its own block because it frees its environment when it goes resident (KEYBCPSD.ASM lines 84-93), leaving a 48-byte hole below itself that later, smaller blocks fill (Lab 8.7 shows it). And BUFFERS=50 /X is the one 4.00 feature that moves a DOS table out of conventional memory: with an EMS 4.0 manager present, SYSINIT puts the buffers into expanded memory pages, two hash buckets of 15 per page, and rounds the count up to whole pages, so 50 becomes 60 (SYSINIT1.ASM lines 2077-2089), under an EMS handle named BUFFERS (SYSINIT1.ASM lines 1069-1076, line 294). Free EMS memory drops by 32 KB, and the BUFFERS= line in MEM by 7,968 bytes to 20h. Without a manager, DoEMS prints the "Error in CONFIG.SYS line" message for the BUFFERS= line, and SYSINIT falls back to the default buffers (SYSINIT1.ASM lines 2126-2132, SYSCONF.ASM lines 2569-2577).

8.3 Expanded memory without a board: EMM386#

What EMM386.SYS is#

The MEMM directory builds EMM386.SYS, which calls itself "MICROSOFT Expanded Memory Manager 386" (EMMMES.ASM lines 92-95). It provides the EMS 4.0 interface of Section 8.1 on any 386 with extended memory, with no board at all. To do that it does something no other part of MS-DOS 4.00 does: it switches the processor to protected mode, sets up a GDT, an IDT, a task state segment and page tables, and then runs DOS, the BIOS and every program in virtual-8086 (V86) mode, a 386 mode in which code behaves like real-mode code but runs under paging and under the control of a protected-mode supervisor. EMM386 is that supervisor, a small virtual machine monitor; the header of its initialisation module says "This module returns to the calling routine in Virtual Mode" (VDMINIT.ASM lines 38-45). Once DOS runs under paging, a 16 KB window of the page frame is just four page-table entries, and "mapping an EMS page" means rewriting them. The design goal is stated at the top of the C part of the manager:

MS-DOS 4.00Listing 8.6 – The idea of EMM386 in one sentence (EMMFUNCT.C lines 43-53)Source ↗
 * Paged EMM Driver for the iAPX 386.
 *
 * The basic concept is to use the 386's page tables to emulate
 * the functions of an EMM board. There are several constraints
 * that are a result of poor planning on the LIM specifiers part.
 *      - maximum of 64K instantaneously mapped. this will
 *        be faithfully emulated in this design
 *      - maximum of 8Mb of extended memory can be used.
 *        The actual reason for this is because each board
 *        can only support 128 16Kb pages and the limit of
 *        4 Aboveboards implies 512 pages maximum. This will

Installation, step by step#

Init_MEMM386 is the device driver's initialisation routine, called by SYSINIT for the DEVICE= line. It is a straight sequence of steps, each of which can set a "killer" message and abandon the installation (INIT.ASM lines 271-610):

Step Routine What it does
1 Inst_chk_f, Is386, VerifyMachine refuse to install twice; check the processor and the machine
2 parser read the DEVICE= parameters: pool size in KB (default 256), Mn page frame, X:mmmm-nnnn exclusions
3 find_phys_pages decide which 16 KB pages below 1 MB may be mapped, and where the page frame goes
4 AllocMem take extended memory for the pool, and the conventional memory above 256 KB
5 EMM_Init, VDM_Init, InitTab build the EMM tables, the GDT, IDT, TSS and page tables
6 IE_chkbase insist that at least 64 KB of conventional memory remain
7 FarGoVirtual enter protected mode and return to DOS in V86 mode
8 IE_exit print the banner and the messages; hook INT 15h and INT 67h

Booting the lab system with DEVICE=\EMM386.SYS and capturing the screen (Lab 8.3) shows the result:

Output 8.2 – EMM386.SYS installing on MS-DOS 4.00 in DOSBox-X (Pentium-class CPU, 16 MB)
MICROSOFT Expanded Memory Manager 386  Version 4.00
(C) Copyright MICROSOFT Corporation 1988
Size of expanded memory pool adjusted.
Page Frame Base Address adjusted.
EMM386 Installed.
                   Extended memory allocated:      256 KB
                   System memory allocated:        384 KB
                                                 --------
                   Expanded memory available:      640 KB
                   Page frame base address:      C4000 H

Every line can be traced to the source. The two "adjusted" messages are not warnings about our machine: the parser sets the size message whenever no size was given and it falls back to 256 KB (INIT.ASM lines 882-886), and find_pf_base sets the page frame message whenever it chose the frame itself (PPAGE.ASM lines 279-290). The frame it chose, C400, follows from step 3:

MS-DOS 4.00Listing 8.7 – Choosing mappable pages: conventional RAM, system ROM, video, option ROMs (PPAGE.ASM lines 150-187)Source ↗
find_phys_pages proc    near
⋮
        call    exclude_conv_RAM
⋮
        call    exclude_system_ROM
⋮
        call    exclude_video_mem
⋮
        call    rom_srch                ; this searches for option rom's and
⋮
;
⋮
find_phys_pages endp

rom_srch looks for the 55 AA signature of option ROMs in 2 KB steps, exactly as the BIOS does at power-on (ROM_SRCH.ASM lines 38-58), and find_pf_base takes the first of the candidate frames C000, C400, … E000 whose four pages are all still mappable (PPAGE.ASM lines 120-136). DOSBox-X's video BIOS is 16 KB long (Lab 8.1 reads its size byte), so C000-C3FF is excluded and C400 is the first free 64 KB. On a real PC with a 32 KB VGA BIOS the same code would pick C800.

The pool comes from extended memory with the INT 15h convention of Section 8.1, top down. EMM386's INT 15h handler answers function 88h with the lowered size:

MS-DOS 4.00Listing 8.8 – EMM386 shrinks extended memory by lying about its size (MOVEB.ASM lines 436-443)Source ↗
        cmp     ah,88h                  ;Q: extended memory size request?
        jne     chk_blk_move            ;  N: go to check for move block call
;
;  Implement int15 allocation scheme by reporting a lowered value of extended
;  memory.
        popf
        mov     ax,cs:[ext_mem_size]    ; report new extended memory size
        iret                            ;

MEM (Lab 8.3) reports 15,056 KB available instead of 15,360: 304 KB are gone. 256 KB are the pool; the other 48 KB hold EMM386's own tables. To keep its conventional-memory footprint small, it "ships" the segments from PAGESEG to LAST (page tables and other large structures) into extended memory, and MEMREQ computes their size and adds 16 KB "for safety" (SHIPHI.ASM lines 305-321; xbuf_chk reserves that first, ALLOCMEM.ASM lines 366-388). What stays below 640 KB is still 37,472 bytes (the DEVICE= line in Lab 8.2), the price of having expanded memory at all.

The "system memory allocated: 384 KB" line is an EMS 4.0 feature. SysAlloc counts every mappable 16 KB page of conventional memory below the INT 12h limit and adds it to the pool (ALLOCMEM.ASM lines 524-551); exclude_conv_RAM has already removed the first 256 KB, segments 0000-4000 (PPAGE.ASM lines 404-429), so pages 4000 to 9C00 remain, 24 pages = 384 KB. These pages belong to handle 0, the operating system's handle, and are mapped where they always were; an EMS 4.0 multitasker could map other pages there and swap whole programs in and out of conventional memory. MEM /DEBUG lists the handle (Lab 8.3).

Mapping a page: four page-table entries and a TLB flush#

With DOS in V86 mode, an INT 67h instruction does not go to the real-mode vector. In V86 mode every interrupt goes through the protected-mode IDT, and EMM386's IDT has a gate for vector 67h, with privilege level 3 so that V86 code may use it:

MS-DOS 4.00Listing 8.9 – The IDT entry for INT 67h (TABDEF.ASM lines 314-315)Source ↗
;;;IDT_ENTRY    0, 0, 0                 ; 67 User Programs
IDT_ENTRY       VDMC_GSEL,<offset _TEXT:EMM_pEntry>,D_386INT3 ; 67 ELIM

EMM_pEntry runs in ring 0, but it does not choose the functions it handles. A program's call finds EMM_Flag clear and is reflected: the monitor builds an interrupt frame on the V86 stack and resumes V86 mode at the real-mode vector, EMM_rEntry. There EMM_rLink runs allocation and the other bookkeeping functions (43h and 45h among them) through the dispatcher in V86 mode. For the functions that change mappings, 44h among them, it sets EMM_Flag and executes INT 67h again, and this time EMM_pEntry calls the function through its own table, in ring 0 (EMM.ASM lines 172-212, lines 213-300, lines 368-429). The header of EMM.ASM promises that protected-mode functions "don't suffer the extra time to reflect the INT 67H" (lines 42-51); in this code every call pays for the reflection, and a mapping call then enters ring 0 a second time. Function 44h itself:

MS-DOS 4.00Listing 8.10 – _MapHandlePage flushes the TLB and maps (EMMP.ASM lines 579-592)Source ↗
_MapHandlePage  proc    near

        Validate_Handle <short mhp_inv_handle>

        mov     byte ptr [bp.rAX+1],OK  ; Assume success!
        movzx   eax, al                 ; Physical page
        movzx   ebx, bx                 ; Logical page

        push    eax
        mov     eax, cr3
        mov     cr3, eax                ; Flush old mapping now
        pop     eax

        jmp     map_page                ; Common page mapping code
MS-DOS 4.00Listing 8.11 – map_EMM_page writes four 4 KB page-table entries for one 16 KB window (EMMP.ASM lines 334-401)Source ↗
map_EMM_page    proc    near
        cmp     ax,[_physical_page_count]       ;Q: valid physical page# ?
        jae     short mEp_inv_page              ;  N: invalid page number
⋮
        add     bx,[_pft386]    ; BX  = points into _pft386
        mov     eax,[bx]        ; EAX = physical address of EMM page #
        and     ax,0F000H       ; clear the low 12 bits
        or      ax,P_AVAIL      ; page ctl bits <-- user,present,write
⋮
        shl     bx,2                    ; bx <-- index * 4
        add     bx,offset DGROUP:_page_frame_base ; bx = offset for entry in _page_frame_base
        les     di,[bx]                 ; es:di <-- page frame address
⋮
        stosd                   ; store 1st page table entry
        add     eax,P_SIZE      ; eax <-- next address

        stosd                   ; store 2nd page table entry
        add     eax,P_SIZE      ; eax <-- next address

        stosd                   ; store 3rd page table entry
        add     eax,P_SIZE      ; eax <-- next address

        stosd                   ; store 4th page table entry

_pft386 holds the physical address of every 16 KB EMS page in the pool; a page-table entry is that address with the low 12 bits replaced by control bits (present, writable, user). Four consecutive entries, 4 KB apart, make one EMS window. Reloading CR3 invalidates the processor's translation lookaside buffer (TLB), so the next access to the window walks the new entries. Notice the order: the flush comes before the entries are written. That is safe only because nothing touches the window's addresses between the two, a detail worth a question (Lab 8.3).

The monitor has other duties that a board never needed. In V86 mode, port I/O to selected ports traps to the monitor, which must emulate it. EMM386 watches the keyboard controller ports that switch A20 and keeps the wrap-around at 1 MB alive with page tables (A20TRAP.ASM); it intercepts the DMA controller, because DMA transfers use physical addresses while V86 programs now use paged ones, and a buffer that is contiguous for the program may not be contiguous in memory. The comment explains it and credits the code to Windows/386 (ELIMTRAP.ASM lines 38-67). Those are the classic problems of every virtual machine monitor, solved in 1988 inside a DOS device driver.

A processor check that never fires#

Step 1 calls Is386, which uses Intel's recommended test on the high bits of the flags register and reports the result in the carry flag:

MS-DOS 4.00Listing 8.12 – Is386 returns CF = 0 for a 386 and CF = 1 otherwise (I286.ASM lines 275-301)Source ↗
Is386   proc    FAR
        push    ax
        pushf                           ; save entry flags
;
        xor     ax,ax                   ; 0000 into AX
        push    ax
        popf                            ; try to put that in the flags
        pushf
        pop     ax                      ; look at what really went into flags
        test    ax,08000h               ;Q: was high bit set ?
        jnz     IsNot386_exit           ;  Y: 8086/8088
        mov     ax,07000h               ;  N: try to set the NT/IOPL bits
        push    ax
        popf                            ;      ... in the flags
        pushf
        pop     ax                      ; look at actual flags
        test    ax,07000h               ; Q: any high bits set ?
        jz      IsNot386_exit           ;   N: 80286
⋮
Is386_exit:
        popf                            ; restore flags
        clc                             ;  386
        jmp     short I386_exit         ; and leave
⋮
IsNot386_exit:
        popf                            ; restore flags
        stc                             ; not a 386

The caller tests a different flag:

MS-DOS 4.00Listing 8.13 – Init_MEMM386 tests ZF after Is386 (INIT.ASM lines 298-308)Source ↗
        call    Inst_chk_f
        or      ax,ax                   ; q: already installed?
        jz      chk_pt                  ; n: go check processor type
        or      [msg_flag],INS_ERR_MSG  ; y: error
        jmp     IE_exit                 ; quit
;
;  verify processor type
;
chk_pt:
        call    Is386                   ;Q: is this a 386 ?
        jnz     inc_prc                 ;  N: no, set error

Is386 restores the flags it saved on entry (popf) and then changes only the carry flag. On entry, the zero flag was set: chk_pt is reached only through jz chk_pt. So after the call ZF is still 1 on every processor, jnz inc_prc is never taken, and the processor test has no effect. What remains is VerifyMachine, which on the installation path only checks that the BIOS model byte at F000:FFFE is FCh ("AT class") (OEMPROC.ASM lines 662-686), and DOSBox-X reports FC whatever processor it emulates.

Swapping jnz for jc is not enough, though. We rebuilt EMM386.SYS from a copy of the tree with exactly that change (the new file differs from the original in two bytes: the jump's opcode and the EXE header checksum), and on an emulated 286 it still hangs before printing its banner. The binary shows why:

Output 8.3 – Conditional jumps in the EMM386.SYS built from source (ndisasm; offsets in the load image, after the 512-byte EXE header)
$ ndisasm -b16 -o 0x70 -e 624 build/dos4/SRC/MEMM/MEMM/EMM386.SYS | head -3
00000070  8A4702            mov al,[bx+0x2]
00000073  3C0D              cmp al,0xd
00000075  0F831F00          jnc 0x98
$ ndisasm -b16 -o 0x4FFD -e 20989 build/dos4/SRC/MEMM/MEMM/EMM386.SYS | head -4
00004FFD  B92500            mov cx,0x25
00005000  FC                cld
00005001  F3A6              repe cmpsb
00005003  0F851000          jnz 0x5017
$ ndisasm -b16 -o 0x14712 -e 84242 build/dos4/SRC/MEMM/MEMM/EMM386.SYS | head -6
00014712  9A6000F804        call word 0x4f8:word 0x60
00014717  0BC0              or ax,ax
00014719  0F840800          jz 0x4725
0001471D  830EC70008        or word [0xc7],0x8
00014722  E94201            jmp 0x4867
00014725  9A60111114        call word 0x1411:word 0x1160
$ ndisasm -b16 -o 0x15278 -e 87160 build/dos4/SRC/MEMM/MEMM/EMM386.SYS | head -2
00015278  A90080            test ax,0x8000
0001527B  0F851200          jnz 0x5291

The four excerpts are, in execution order: the device driver's interrupt routine checking the request's command code (cmp al,TBL_LENGTH / jae Invalid, MEMM386.ASM lines 307-309); Inst_chk, which compares a signature to find out whether EMM386 is already installed (lines 499-531); Listing 8.13 (call Inst_chk_f, or ax,ax, jz chk_pt, …, call Is386); and the first test inside Is386. Every conditional jump is encoded as 0F 8x with a 16-bit displacement: the near form of Jcc that the 386 introduced. The 8086 and the 286 have only the 2-byte short form (7x and an 8-bit displacement), which would have been enough, since every target is less than 40 bytes away. The modules are assembled with .386p (MEMM386.ASM line 133, INIT.ASM line 48, I286.ASM line 84), and in that mode MASM 5.10 encoded these forward jumps in the long form. On a 286, 0F 83, 0F 84 and 0F 85 are not valid instructions, so the very first conditional jump the driver executes, at offset 75h of its interrupt routine, raises the invalid-opcode exception (interrupt 6), long before Init_MEMM386 reaches its processor test; on the emulated 286 the boot gets no further (we did not trace where exactly it loops). On an 8086, 0F is POP CS, with no better outcome. Is386 is correct 8086 source code and the sequence Intel recommended; the bytes the assembler produced from it are not 8086 code. Exercise 8.4 asks you to reproduce both faults and to repair the driver so that a 286 gets the "incorrect machine type" message; it can be done by changing a handful of jumps, and the repaired driver, rebuilt with the 1988 tools, prints the message on the emulated 286 and lets the boot continue.

8.4 FreeBSD memory in practice#

Physical memory and the page queues#

A FreeBSD process never sees physical addresses (Module 2, Section 2.5). Physical memory is a pool of 4 KB pages that the kernel hands out on demand, and the administrator's question "where did my memory go?" is answered by counting pages by state. The kernel's view of the machine starts with three sysctl variables:

FreeBSD 15.1Listing 8.14 – hw.physmem: usable physical memory, in bytes (kern_mib.c lines 200-213)Source ↗
sysctl_hw_physmem(SYSCTL_HANDLER_ARGS)
{
        u_long val, p;

        p = SIZE_T_MAX >> PAGE_SHIFT;
        if (physmem < p)
                p = physmem;
        val = ctob(p);
        return (sysctl_handle_long(oidp, &val, 0, req));
}
SYSCTL_PROC(_hw, HW_PHYSMEM, physmem,
    CTLTYPE_ULONG | CTLFLAG_RD | CTLFLAG_MPSAFE, 0, 0,
    sysctl_hw_physmem, "LU",
    "Amount of physical memory (in bytes)");

hw.realmem is what the firmware reported, hw.physmem what the kernel uses, and hw.usermem the part that is not wired (lines 216-245). hw.physmem is also a loader tunable: hammer_time() reads it before the VM system exists and lowers Maxmem (machdep.c lines 921-922), so hw.physmem="1G" in loader.conf makes a large machine behave like a small one, the FreeBSD way to emulate a smaller INT 12h.

Every managed page is in one of a few states. Free pages sit in the physical allocator's free lists. Pages that belong to a VM object (a file's cached data, or a process's anonymous memory) sit in one of the page queues:

FreeBSD 15.1Listing 8.15 – The page queues (vm_page.h lines 322-327)Source ↗
#define PQ_NONE         255
#define PQ_INACTIVE     0
#define PQ_ACTIVE       1
#define PQ_LAUNDRY      2
#define PQ_UNSWAPPABLE  3
#define PQ_COUNT        4

Active pages were used recently. The page daemon (vm_pageout.c) scans the active queue and moves pages that have not been referenced to inactive. A clean inactive page (its contents are also in a file or in swap) can be freed at once when memory is short; a dirty one must be written first, so it goes to the laundry queue, from which the laundry thread writes anonymous pages to swap. Wired pages (kernel memory, mlock(2), page tables) are in no queue at all and cannot be paged out. There is no separate "file cache": the cache is simply the vnode-backed pages in these queues, which is why a FreeBSD system that has been running for a while shows little "Free" memory and that is good, not bad.

The counters are exported read-only under vm.stats.vm:

FreeBSD 15.1Listing 8.16 – Page counts as sysctl variables (vm_meter.c lines 383-395)Source ↗
VM_STATS_UINT(v_page_size, "Page size in bytes");
VM_STATS_UINT(v_page_count, "Total number of pages in system");
VM_STATS_UINT(v_free_reserved, "Pages reserved for deadlock");
VM_STATS_UINT(v_free_target, "Pages desired free");
VM_STATS_UINT(v_free_min, "Minimum low-free-pages threshold");
VM_STATS_PROC(v_free_count, "Free pages", vm_free_count);
VM_STATS_PROC(v_wire_count, "Wired pages", vm_wire_count);
VM_STATS_PROC(v_nofree_count, "Permanently allocated pages", vm_nofree_count);
VM_STATS_PROC(v_active_count, "Active pages", vm_active_count);
VM_STATS_UINT(v_inactive_target, "Desired inactive pages");
VM_STATS_PROC(v_inactive_count, "Inactive pages", vm_inactive_count);
VM_STATS_PROC(v_laundry_count, "Pages eligible for laundering",
    vm_laundry_count);

The tools are thin layers over these variables. top's memory line, "Active, Inact, Laundry, Wired, Buf, Free", is these counts converted to KB:

FreeBSD 15.1Listing 8.17 – top reads the page counts with sysctl (machine.c lines 567-572)Source ↗
                GETSYSCTL("vfs.bufspace", bufspace);
                GETSYSCTL("vm.stats.vm.v_active_count", memory_stats[0]);
                GETSYSCTL("vm.stats.vm.v_inactive_count", memory_stats[1]);
                GETSYSCTL("vm.stats.vm.v_laundry_count", memory_stats[2]);
                GETSYSCTL("vm.stats.vm.v_wire_count", memory_stats[3]);
                GETSYSCTL("vm.stats.vm.v_free_count", memory_stats[5]);

vmstat reads the same counters (its struct mirrors vm_cnt, vmstat.c lines 125-151), swapinfo (another name for pstat -s, swapinfo(8)) lists the swap devices, and procstat -v shows one process's map entries (Module 2, Study case 2.C). Lab 8.6 uses all of them.

Question MS-DOS 4.00 FreeBSD 15.1
How much memory is there? INT 12h, MEM "total memory" sysctl hw.physmem hw.realmem
How much is free? MEM "largest executable program size" sysctl vm.stats.vm.v_free_count, top "Free"
Who uses it? MEM /PROGRAM: one line per arena block top -o res, ps -o rss,vsz, procstat -v
What is the kernel using? MEM "System Data", IO, MSDOS vm.stats.vm.v_wire_count, vmstat -m, vmstat -z
Extra memory MEM: extended and EMS lines swap: swapinfo, vm.swap_total

Swap, overcommit and the OOM killer#

A FreeBSD malloc of 1 GB usually succeeds on a machine with 512 MB: the kernel only creates a map entry, and pages arrive on first touch. What it does account for is swap reservation: every page of anonymous memory might one day have to go to swap, so the kernel adds it to swap_reserved and compares with swap_total. Whether it refuses is a policy, set by the vm.overcommit sysctl ("See tuning(7)", swap_pager.c lines 178-181):

FreeBSD 15.1Listing 8.18 – Swap reservation and the overcommit bits (swap_pager.c lines 289-304)Source ↗
        pincr = atop(incr);
        prev = atomic_fetchadd_long(&swap_reserved, pincr);
        r = prev + pincr;
        s = swap_total;
        oc = atomic_load_int(&vm_overcommit);
        if (r > s && (oc & SWAP_RESERVE_ALLOW_NONWIRED) != 0) {
                s += vm_cnt.v_page_count - vm_cnt.v_free_reserved -
                    vm_wire_count();
        }
        if ((oc & SWAP_RESERVE_FORCE_ON) != 0 && r > s &&
            priv_check(curthread, PRIV_VM_SWAP_NOQUOTA) != 0) {
                prev = atomic_fetchadd_long(&swap_reserved, -pincr);
                KASSERT(prev >= pincr,
                    ("swap_reserved < incr on overcommit fail"));
                goto out_error;
        }

The default, vm.overcommit=0, never fails here: memory is overcommitted. Even with bit 0 (SWAP_RESERVE_FORCE_ON) set, the refusal applies only to threads that fail priv_check(..., PRIV_VM_SWAP_NOQUOTA); root holds that privilege, so a root process is never refused, and an experiment with vm.overcommit=1 must run as an ordinary user (Lab 8.6). The price is paid later, if programs actually touch more pages than RAM plus swap can hold. Then the page daemon cannot find pages to free; after vm.pageout_oom_seq (12 by default) consecutive failed passes (vm_pageout.c lines 182-185) it calls vm_pageout_oom(), which walks all processes, skips system processes, init (pid 1) and, while some swap space is still free (swap_pager_avail != 0), every process with a pid below 48 (lines 1975-1984), and kills the largest:

FreeBSD 15.1Listing 8.19 – The out-of-memory killer picks the biggest process (vm_pageout.c lines 2045-2063)Source ↗
        if (bigproc != NULL) {
                switch (shortage) {
                case VM_OOM_MEM:
                        reason = "failed to reclaim memory";
                        break;
                case VM_OOM_MEM_PF:
                        reason = "a thread waited too long to allocate a page";
                        break;
                case VM_OOM_SWAPZ:
                        reason = "out of swap space";
                        break;
                default:
                        panic("unknown OOM reason %d", shortage);
                }
                if (vm_panic_on_oom != 0 && --vm_panic_on_oom == 0)
                        panic("%s", reason);
                PROC_LOCK(bigproc);
                killproc(bigproc, reason);
                sched_nice(bigproc, PRIO_MIN);

The contrast with MS-DOS is complete. DOS refuses an allocation at once and exactly (error 8, with the largest free size in BX); nothing is ever taken back from a program that holds memory. FreeBSD says yes almost always, finds out later that it cannot keep the promise, and then takes memory back by force, from a process that may not be the one that caused the shortage.

8.5 Allocating memory from a program#

MS-DOS: INT 21h function 48h and the Microsoft C heap#

A DOS program gets memory in paragraphs from the arena with function 48h (Module 2, Section 2.5). Most programs were written in C, though, and called malloc, so what a program could allocate depended as much on the C library as on DOS. Microsoft C 5.10, the compiler in the MS-DOS 4.00 tree, has memory models: in the small model, code and data have one 64 KB segment each, pointers are 16 bits, and malloc is _nmalloc, which allocates from the near heap inside the data segment (DGROUP); _fmalloc allocates from the far heap, segments obtained from DOS. In the large model, pointers are 32 bits (segment:offset) and malloc is _fmalloc. The library's malloc.h shows the names (_nmalloc, _fmalloc, _memavl, _memmax, halloc; it is in TOOLS/BLD/INC, part of the release but not a source file of DOS).

Lab 8.4 builds one program in both models and lets it allocate 1 KB blocks until malloc returns NULL:

Output 8.4 – HEAP.EXE in the small and the large model on MS-DOS 4.00 (built with Microsoft C 5.10)
---- HEAPS
model: small, sizeof(char *) = 2, PSP at segment 1204
at start:                    DOS largest free block 509072 bytes
near heap:                   _memavl()  60716 bytes, _memmax() 60716
malloc(1024) succeeded 59 times: 60416 bytes; first block at 13B6:12D2
after malloc:                DOS largest free block 509072 bytes
then _fmalloc(1024) succeeded 493 times: 504832 bytes
after _fmalloc:              DOS largest free block      0 bytes
---- HEAPL
model: large, sizeof(char *) = 4, PSP at segment 1204
at start:                    DOS largest free block 508144 bytes
near heap:                   _memavl()  60230 bytes, _memmax() 60230
malloc(1024) succeeded 550 times: 563200 bytes; first block at 23F1:000C
after malloc:                DOS largest free block      0 bytes
then _fmalloc(1024) succeeded 0 times: 0 bytes
after _fmalloc:              DOS largest free block      0 bytes

Three things are visible. First, a small-model program cannot malloc more than about 60 KB on a machine with 580 KB free: the near heap is bounded by the 64 KB segment, and the rest is reachable only with far pointers. Second, the C start-up code reserves the whole 64 KB data segment at start: DOS's largest free block does not change while the near heap fills up. The arithmetic proves it: the program's block is 581,568 - 509,072 - 16 = 72,480 bytes, exactly 256 (PSP) + 6,688 (code, from the link map) + 65,536 (DGROUP). By default every EXE that LINK produces asks for the maximum (e_maxalloc = FFFFh in the header), DOS gives it the largest block, and the run-time shrinks it to what it wants. Third, the large-model malloc takes everything: 563,200 bytes, more than DOS had free, because it used DOS segments and the near heap.

FreeBSD: jemalloc over mmap#

FreeBSD's malloc is jemalloc, compiled into libc. The release's libc.so.7 exports it together with its tuning interface, and depends on libsys.so.7, which contains the system call stubs (readelf -d, nm -D on the real files):

Output 8.5 – Allocation symbols in FreeBSD 15.1's libc.so.7 and libsys.so.7 (GNU nm on the release files)
$ nm -D --defined-only lib/libc.so.7 | grep -E ' (malloc|free|sbrk|brk|malloc_conf|_malloc_options|malloc_stats_print|mallctl)@'
000000000020c680 B _malloc_options@FBSD_1.0
0000000000144f90 T brk@@FBSD_1.0
00000000001872d0 W free@@FBSD_1.0
000000000018b0c0 W mallctl@@FBSD_1.3
00000000001854f0 W malloc@@FBSD_1.0
0000000000214720 V malloc_conf@@FBSD_1.3
000000000018b280 W malloc_stats_print@@FBSD_1.3
00000000001450b0 T sbrk@@FBSD_1.0
$ readelf -d lib/libc.so.7 | grep -E 'NEEDED|SONAME'
 0x0000000000000001 (NEEDED)             Shared library: [libsys.so.7]
 0x000000000000000e (SONAME)             Library soname: [libc.so.7]
$ nm -D --defined-only lib/libsys.so.7 | grep -E ' (mmap|munmap|madvise)@'
00000000000183c0 W madvise@@FBSD_1.0
000000000001a1a0 W mmap@@FBSD_1.0
0000000000018380 W munmap@@FBSD_1.0

brk and sbrk are still exported, but jemalloc does not use them on FreeBSD. The generic configuration defines JEMALLOC_DSS (use the data segment, that is sbrk), and FreeBSD's override file undefines it again:

FreeBSD 15.1Listing 8.20 – FreeBSD's jemalloc build: no sbrk, no background threads (jemalloc_FreeBSD.h lines 1-15)Source ↗
/*
 * Override settings that were generated in jemalloc_defs.h as necessary.
 */

#ifndef JEMALLOC_NO_PRIVATE_NAMESPACE

#undef JEMALLOC_OVERRIDE_VALLOC

#ifndef MALLOC_PRODUCTION
#define JEMALLOC_DEBUG
#endif

#undef JEMALLOC_DSS

#undef JEMALLOC_BACKGROUND_THREAD

The override wins because jemalloc_preamble.h includes the generated definitions first and jemalloc.h (which includes this file) afterwards, and only then computes have_dss (jemalloc_preamble.h lines 1-35, lines 72-78). So malloc gets all its memory with mmap(2), never with sbrk (Lab 8.6's truss shows no break call). The same generated file shows JEMALLOC_STATS enabled and a hook that reads FreeBSD's vm.overcommit sysctl (jemalloc_internal_defs.h lines 147-148, lines 269-275).

Giving memory back is more subtle. FreeBSD's jemalloc runs with opt.retain set (Lab 8.6 prints it), because the override file defines JEMALLOC_RETAIN whenever virtual addresses are wider than 32 bits (jemalloc_FreeBSD.h lines 83-85). jemalloc(3) describes the option as "retain unused virtual memory for later reuse rather than discarding it by calling munmap(2)" (jemalloc.3 lines 872-882): the address range stays mapped. Freed pages are purged with madvise(..., MADV_FREE), and that does not unmap them either. vm_page_advise only marks each page clean and puts it near the head of the inactive queue, because "MADV_FREE pages are often quickly reused by malloc(3), so we do not do anything that would result in a page fault on a later access" (vm_page.c lines 4635-4668). The pages stay in the process's resident set until the page daemon needs them, and then it can free them without writing anything to swap.

That MADV_FREE is a consequence of the default vm.overcommit=0. For a freed extent that it retains, jemalloc first tries to decommit it, then to purge it by force, and only then purges it lazily (extent.c lines 1053-1069). On FreeBSD the first two both end in pages_commit_impl, which refuses when the system overcommits (pages.c lines 349-356, lines 466-489), so the lazy purge, madvise(MADV_FREE), does the work (lines 428-464). jemalloc decides this once, at start-up, from a flag that the kernel puts in the ELF auxiliary vector only if bit 0 or 1 of vm.overcommit is set (pages.c lines 591-618, imgact_elf.c lines 1500-1505). A program started while one of those bits is set decommits instead: it maps fresh PROT_NONE memory over the range with MAP_FIXED (pages.c lines 320-347), which replaces the old pages (mmap.2 lines 199-209).

jemalloc is configured at run time by a string of option:value pairs. The malloc(3) page of the release says where the string comes from: "The string specified via --with-malloc-conf, the string pointed to by the global variable malloc_conf, the 'name' of the file referenced by the symbolic link named /etc/malloc.conf, and the value of the environment variable MALLOC_CONF, will be interpreted, in that order, from left to right as options." Two options matter in Lab 8.6: stats_print:true prints statistics at exit, and dirty_decay_ms (default 10 seconds) controls how long freed pages stay dirty before jemalloc purges them; the second stage, muzzy_decay_ms, defaults to 0 (arena_types.h lines 6-8). Because FreeBSD's build has no background threads, that purge happens only when the program calls the allocator again. Requests of opt.oversize_threshold (8 MiB) or more are the exception. jemalloc(3) says that requests with "greater sizes" are served by a dedicated arena, and that "the decay API guarantees on the extents greater than the specified threshold may be overridden" (jemalloc.3 lines 909-914). The source compares with >=, so a malloc of exactly 8 MiB goes there too (arena_types.h lines 38-42, arena_inlines_b.h lines 20-39, called with the requested size from arena.c lines 1190-1206). That arena takes the index after the automatic arenas (arena.c lines 1744-1762). It is created on first use, and if the default decay times are positive they are set to 0 for it, to "Purge eagerly for huge allocations" (lines 1725-1738). With a decay time of 0 the purge happens inside free itself. The freed extent goes into the dirty cache as "deferred work", and arena_handle_deferred_work purges the whole cache before free returns (large.c lines 250-257, pac.c lines 277-279, arena.c lines 213-224, decay.h lines 121-125). Lab 8.6's statistics show the result: decay time 0 for that arena, and one madvise for the whole block.

MS-DOS 4.00 + Microsoft C 5.10 FreeBSD 15.1
Kernel interface INT 21h 48h/49h/4Ah, paragraphs mmap and madvise (jemalloc keeps its address ranges), pages
Library near heap in DGROUP (small model), far heap from DOS jemalloc in libc, arenas and thread caches
Pointer 16-bit near or 32-bit segment:offset 64-bit virtual address
Out of memory malloc returns NULL, immediately and exactly malloc rarely fails; touching pages may trigger the OOM killer
Freed memory stays in the program's heap until exit purged with madvise(MADV_FREE) after dirty_decay_ms (at once from 8 MiB up); resident until the page daemon takes it
Tuning memory model at compile time; /CP option of LINK sets e_maxalloc MALLOC_CONF, /etc/malloc.conf, malloc_conf

8.6 Configuring MS-DOS#

Two text files, two interpreters#

An MS-DOS 4.00 system is configured by two plain text files in the root directory of the boot disk, read by two different programs at two different moments (Figure 8.5):

  • CONFIG.SYS is read once by SYSINIT before any shell exists (Module 1, Section 1.5). Its keywords are reduced to one-letter codes and processed in several passes: DEVICE= drivers before INSTALL= programs, whatever their order in the file. It decides what lives in conventional memory for the whole session: the kernel's tables (BUFFERS=, FILES=, FCBS=, STACKS=, LASTDRIVE=), the drivers (DEVICE=, IFS=), the resident programs (INSTALL=), the shell (SHELL=) and the national conventions (COUNTRY=).
  • AUTOEXEC.BAT is an ordinary batch file that COMMAND.COM runs because it was started with /P (Module 3, Section 3.6). It sets the environment (PATH, PROMPT, SET), starts resident programs (KEYB, PRINT, FASTOPEN, GRAPHICS) and runs MODE to configure devices.

A 1988 configuration for a 386 with 1 MB of extended memory, Italian keyboard and a RAM disk might read:

Text
COUNTRY=039,437,\COUNTRY.SYS
BUFFERS=20
FILES=30
LASTDRIVE=E
DEVICE=\ANSI.SYS
DEVICE=\EMM386.SYS 512
DEVICE=\RAMDRIVE.SYS 256 /A
SHELL=\COMMAND.COM \ /P /E:512
Batch file
@ECHO OFF
PROMPT $P$G
PATH A:\;C:\
SET TEMP=C:\
KEYB IT,437,\KEYBOARD.SYS
MODE COM1:9600,N,8,1

Every line has a price in conventional memory that Section 8.2 lets you compute, and none can be changed without a reboot except those in AUTOEXEC.BAT, which can simply be typed again.

National support: COUNTRY=, KEYB and MODE#

COUNTRY= selects the date, time and number formats that INT 21h function 38h returns (GETSET.ASM lines 147-186) and the case-mapping and collating tables that function 65h returns (DOSCNTRY.INC lines 1-10); SYSINIT reads the data from COUNTRY.SYS. KEYB replaces the BIOS keyboard handler with one that translates scan codes according to a layout from KEYBOARD.SYS; it is a TSR, so loading it at run time costs memory that is never given back (Lab 8.7 measures 5,792 bytes), and KEYB US later only switches the active layout. MODE configures serial ports, printers, the console and code pages; it changes BIOS or driver state and exits. Code-page switching (DEVICE=\DISPLAY.SYS, NLSFUNC, MODE CON CP PREPARE) is the most complex part of 4.00's configuration and is out of scope here.

Where the configuration lives at run time#

Nowhere, as such. There is no file that records "the current configuration", and no system call that changes it. What CONFIG.SYS asked for exists only as tables in the owner-8 block (Section 8.2) and as resident drivers; the environment lives in COMMAND.COM's environment block (Module 3, Section 3.7); MODE's settings live in the BIOS data area or in a driver. MEM /PROGRAM is the closest thing to a configuration viewer, and it works by walking memory.

8.7 Configuring FreeBSD#

FreeBSD's configuration is split by who reads it and when. The loader reads /boot/loader.conf before the kernel runs; the kernel reads tunables from the loader's environment while it starts; init runs /etc/rc, which reads /etc/rc.conf and runs the scripts in /etc/rc.d in an order computed by rcorder; other daemons and programs read their own files (/etc/fstab, /etc/ttys, /etc/login.conf, /etc/sysctl.conf). Almost every file comes in two layers: a defaults file that the system owns and updates, and a small local file that contains only the differences. All configuration files quoted below are the files of the 15.1 release (base.txz), which are identical to the source files at the pinned commit.

loader.conf: variables, tunables, modules#

Module 1 (Section 1.4) showed how the Lua loader reads loader_conf_files. Its defaults file, /boot/defaults/loader.conf, contains three kinds of lines: settings for the loader itself (kernel=, autoboot_delay=), lines that load modules (name_load="YES"), and kernel tunables, which the loader passes to the kernel in its environment. The defaults file lists the classic tunables, all commented out:

FreeBSD 15.1Listing 8.21 – Kernel tunables in the default loader.conf (loader.conf lines 151-160)Source ↗
###  Kernel tunables  ########################################
#hw.physmem="1G"                # Limit physical memory. See loader(8)
#kern.dfldsiz=""                # Set the initial data size limit
#kern.dflssiz=""                # Set the initial stack size limit
#kern.hz="100"                  # Set the kernel interval timer rate
#kern.maxbcache=""              # Set the max buffer cache KVA storage
#kern.maxdsiz=""                # Set the max data size
#kern.maxfiles=""               # Set the sys. wide open files limit
#kern.maxproc=""                # Set the maximum # of processes
#kern.maxssiz=""                # Set the max stack size

kern.maxfiles is the FreeBSD counterpart of FILES=. It is not a table size chosen by the administrator but a limit computed from the memory size, which a tunable may override:

FreeBSD 15.1Listing 8.22 – kern.maxfiles: 32 open files per MB of RAM by default (subr_param.c lines 318-326)Source ↗
         * 'maxfiles' by default is set to 32 files per MB (overridable by
         * a tunable), and is then clamped at 64 files per MB (which thus never
         * happens by default).  (The default MAXFILES is for all practical
         * purposes not used, as it gives a lower value than 32 files per MB as
         * soon as there is more than ~2.5MB of memory.)
         */
        maxfiles = imax(MAXFILES, pgtok(physpages) / (1024 / 32));
        TUNABLE_INT_FETCH("kern.maxfiles", &maxfiles);
        maxfiles_clamp = pgtok(physpages) / (1024 / 64);

In the course's 2 GB virtual machine sysctl kern.maxfiles prints 64305: hw.physmem is 2,107,146,240 bytes, that is 514,440 pages or 2,057,760 KB, and 2,057,760 / 32 = 64,305. Since struct file objects are allocated on demand (Module 2, Section 2.3), the limit costs nothing until it is used. The FILES= table, in contrast, is allocated in full at boot whether files are opened or not.

rc.conf and rc.subr: defaults plus overrides#

/etc/defaults/rc.conf (795 lines in 15.1) assigns a default to every variable the base system's scripts use, for example sshd_enable="NO", cron_enable="YES", syslogd_enable="YES" and dumpdev="NO". Its line 75 names the files that override it, rc_conf_files="/etc/rc.conf /etc/rc.conf.local", and the file ends by defining source_rc_confs, which sources them (rc.conf line 75, lines 757-789). The files are shell scripts; "reading the configuration" means running them with . in the current shell, so a later assignment wins. load_rc_config in rc.subr does it once per shell:

FreeBSD 15.1Listing 8.23 – load_rc_config: defaults first, then the local files (rc.subr lines 1988-2000)Source ↗
        if ${_rc_conf_loaded:-false}; then
                :
        else
                if [ -r /etc/defaults/rc.conf ]; then
                        debug "Sourcing /etc/defaults/rc.conf"
                        $_dot /etc/defaults/rc.conf
                        source_rc_confs
                elif [ -r /etc/rc.conf ]; then
                        debug "Sourcing /etc/rc.conf (/etc/defaults/rc.conf doesn't exist)."
                        $_dot /etc/rc.conf
                fi
                _rc_conf_loaded=true
        fi

When a script passes its name, load_rc_config also sources /etc/rc.conf.d/<name> (or every file in that directory), so one service's settings can live in a file of their own (lines 2002-2021). Boolean values go through checkyesno, which accepts YES, TRUE, ON and 1 in any case as yes and NO, FALSE, OFF and 0 as no; anything else also counts as no, with the warning "is not set properly - see rc.conf(5)" (lines 327-347). The rc.conf(5) page of the release states the contract: "Options need only be specified in /etc/rc.conf when the system administrator wishes to override these defaults." The sysrc(8) utility edits these files safely from scripts (sysrc sshd_enable=YES).

/etc/rc and rcorder: ordering by declared dependencies#

init runs /etc/rc (Module 3), which loads the configuration and then runs the rc.d scripts in two passes:

FreeBSD 15.1Listing 8.24 – /etc/rc runs rcorder twice, split at early_late_divider (rc lines 98-124)Source ↗
# Do a first pass to get everything up to $early_late_divider so that
# we can do a second pass that includes $local_startup directories
#
unset system_rc
find_system_scripts
files=`rcorder ${skip} ${skip_firstboot} ${system_rc} 2>/dev/null`
run_rc_scripts --break ${early_late_divider} ${rc_early_flags} $files
⋮
find_system_scripts
files=`rcorder ${skip} ${skip_firstboot} ${system_rc} ${local_rc} 2>/dev/null`
run_rc_scripts ${rc_late_flags} $files

The first pass runs the base system's scripts up to early_late_divider, which defaults to FILESYSTEMS (rc.conf line 35): until the local file systems are mounted, /usr/local/etc/rc.d (where packages put their scripts) may not even exist. The second pass orders all scripts again, now including the local ones, and runs those not yet run. ${skip} contains -s nostart and, inside a jail, -s nojail (plus -s nojailvnet if the jail has no virtual network stack of its own) (lines 85-91).

rcorder computes the order from a comment block at the top of every script. The rules are in rcorder(8): each line must start with # PROVIDE:, # REQUIRE:, # BEFORE: or # KEYWORD:, and "once a line that does not follow the format is reached, parsing stops" (crunch_file, rcorder.c lines 472-541). PROVIDE names conditions; REQUIRE names conditions that must be provided first; BEFORE: X makes this script a requirement of every provider of X (insert_before, lines 591-627). Some scripts exist only to provide a milestone: FILESYSTEMS, NETWORKING, SERVERS, DAEMON and LOGIN contain only their header and a comment ("This is a dummy dependency"). Lab 8.5 lists the real headers of eleven scripts (Output 8.13).

The algorithm is a depth-first topological sort. do_file first satisfies every requirement of a script (recursively running do_file on the providers), then assigns the script a sequence number one higher than the highest sequence among those providers:

FreeBSD 15.1Listing 8.25 – rcorder 15.1 numbers scripts by dependency depth (rcorder.c lines 913-924)Source ↗
        r = fnode->req_list;
        fnode->sequence = 0;
        while (r != NULL) {
                satisfy_req(r, fnode, stack_ptr);
                /* find sequence number where all requirements are satisfied */
                head = Hash_GetValue(r->entry);
                if (head && head->sequence > fnode->sequence)
                        fnode->sequence = head->sequence;
                r = r->next;
        }
        fnode->req_list = NULL;
        fnode->sequence++;

generate_ordering then sorts the scripts by that number with qsort and prints them, one per line, or with -p all scripts of one sequence number on one line: scripts on the same line could run in parallel (lines 1072-1110). Lab 8.5 runs this algorithm by hand and with a Python model on the 171 real scripts.

rc.d scripts and rc.subr#

An rc.d script is a shell script with a header for rcorder, a few variables, and one call. This is the whole of the base system's rwho script:

FreeBSD 15.1Listing 8.26 – A complete rc.d script (rwho lines 1-20)Source ↗
#!/bin/sh
#
#

# PROVIDE: rwho
# REQUIRE: DAEMON
# BEFORE:  LOGIN
# KEYWORD: shutdown

. /etc/rc.subr

name="rwhod"
desc="System status server"
rcvar="rwhod_enable"
command="/usr/sbin/${name}"

: ${rwhod_svcj_options:="net_basic"}

load_rc_config $name
run_rc_command "$1"

run_rc_command implements start, stop, restart, status, enable, disable and the rest. It starts $command $command_args only if checkyesno $rcvar succeeds (rwhod_enable is NO in the defaults), and it finds a running instance through pidfile, or by matching the process name in ps output when there is none (check_pidfile, check_process, rc.subr lines 420-555). At boot, /etc/rc calls each script with faststart, or with quietstart when init did not pass it autoboot, as after single-user mode (rc lines 49-56, rc.subr lines 1906-1942); an administrator uses service(8), which "will set the same restricted environment that is in use at boot time" (service(8)): service rwho start, service sshd restart, service -e to list the enabled services. Lab 8.5 writes a script for a toy daemon.

sysctl.conf, fstab, ttys, login.conf#

/etc/rc.d/sysctl runs early (it requires nothing) and applies /etc/sysctl.conf and /etc/sysctl.conf.local with sysctl -i -f, which ignores variables that do not exist yet; its lastload command applies them again late in the boot, with plain -f, for variables that only exist after a module has been loaded (sysctl lines 9-34). The release's /etc/sysctl.conf contains only comments: by default nothing is changed. /etc/fstab is not in base.txz at all; the installer writes it, and fstab(5) describes its fields. /etc/ttys tells init which terminals get a getty: on 15.1 ttyv0 to ttyv7 "onifexists" and the serial line ttyu0 "onifconsole" (ttys lines 26-40). /etc/login.conf sets per-class resource limits that login applies; the default class of the release sets datasize, stacksize, memoryuse, openfiles, maxproc, vmemoryuse and swapuse to unlimited, and contains commented-out examples of tighter classes (lines 24-49 of the real file; its source is not in the course's sparse checkout).

Mechanism by mechanism#

Purpose MS-DOS 4.00 FreeBSD 15.1
Size kernel tables BUFFERS=, FILES=, FCBS=, STACKS=, LASTDRIVE= mostly automatic; tunables in loader.conf (kern.maxfiles, kern.maxproc)
Limit memory none (INT 12h from the BIOS) hw.physmem in loader.conf
Load drivers DEVICE=, IFS= in CONFIG.SYS name_load="YES" in loader.conf, kld_list in rc.conf, kldload
Start resident programs INSTALL= in CONFIG.SYS, TSRs in AUTOEXEC.BAT rc.d scripts enabled with name_enable="YES"
Order of start-up position in the file, plus fixed passes PROVIDE/REQUIRE/BEFORE and rcorder
Choose the shell SHELL= /etc/passwd, chsh; init_shell for single-user mode
Environment, search path SET, PATH, PROMPT in AUTOEXEC.BAT shell start-up files, /etc/login.conf (setenv, path)
National conventions COUNTRY=, KEYB, MODE CON CP locale environment variables, keymap= in rc.conf
Devices MODE, DRIVPARM= /etc/ttys, stty, devfs.rules, sysctl
File systems drive letters, LASTDRIVE=, SUBST, JOIN /etc/fstab, mount
Kernel parameters at run time none sysctl, /etc/sysctl.conf
Per-user limits none /etc/login.conf

8.8 Boot-time and run-time configuration#

On MS-DOS the line between the two is simple: everything in CONFIG.SYS needs a reboot, because SYSINIT allocates the tables once, in the owner-8 block, and no system call can grow or shrink them. What changes at run time is what a program can change by itself: the environment (SET, PATH, PROMPT), device state (MODE), and the set of resident programs, which can only grow. A TSR loaded at the prompt stays until the next reboot unless it implements its own unloading, and even then only if nothing was loaded after it.

FreeBSD distinguishes four cases, and the kernel enforces the first two:

FreeBSD 15.1Listing 8.27 – Readable, writable, tunable: the sysctl flags (sysctl.h lines 81-93)Source ↗
#define CTLFLAG_RD      0x80000000      /* Allow reads of variable */
#define CTLFLAG_WR      0x40000000      /* Allow writes to the variable */
#define CTLFLAG_RW      (CTLFLAG_RD|CTLFLAG_WR)
#define CTLFLAG_DORMANT 0x20000000      /* This sysctl is not active yet */
#define CTLFLAG_ANYBODY 0x10000000      /* All users can set this var */
#define CTLFLAG_SECURE  0x08000000      /* Permit set only if securelevel<=0 */
#define CTLFLAG_PRISON  0x04000000      /* Prisoned roots can fiddle */
#define CTLFLAG_DYN     0x02000000      /* Dynamic oid - can be freed */
#define CTLFLAG_SKIP    0x01000000      /* Skip this sysctl when listing */
#define CTLMASK_SECURE  0x00F00000      /* Secure level */
#define CTLFLAG_TUN     0x00080000      /* Default value is loaded from getenv() */
#define CTLFLAG_RDTUN   (CTLFLAG_RD|CTLFLAG_TUN)
#define CTLFLAG_RWTUN   (CTLFLAG_RW|CTLFLAG_TUN)
  1. Read-only tunables (CTLFLAG_RDTUN, or plain TUNABLE_*_FETCH calls such as hw.physmem): set in loader.conf, read once while the kernel starts; changing them needs a reboot, as on DOS.
  2. Run-time sysctls (CTLFLAG_RW): sysctl vm.overcommit=1 takes effect immediately; put the same line in /etc/sysctl.conf to make it permanent. CTLFLAG_RWTUN variables such as kern.maxfiles (kern_descrip.c line 5398) and vm.pageout_oom_seq can be set either way. sysctl(8) has -T to "display only variables that are settable via loader (CTLFLAG_TUN)" and -W to "display only writable variables that are not statistical". Both filter a listing, so they need -a or variable names: sysctl -aT lists 855 tunables in the course VM, while a bare sysctl -T only prints the usage message (sysctl.c lines 243-248).
  3. Services: a change in rc.conf takes effect when the service is next started; service name restart applies it without a reboot.
  4. Modules: kldload and kldunload add and remove kernel code at run time; loader.conf and kld_list make the choice permanent.

The cost of a mistake follows from the same design. A misspelled keyword in CONFIG.SYS costs one line: SYSINIT prints "Unrecognized command in CONFIG.SYS" and "Error in CONFIG.SYS line n" and goes on (Module 1, Exercise 1.4). A wrong SHELL= stops the machine in STALL: JMP STALL (Listing 1.16). A driver that corrupts memory, or claims the same extended memory as another, fails much later and somewhere else. On FreeBSD a wrong value in rc.conf usually affects one service: checkyesno warns and treats the value as "no", rcorder warns about a requirement that has no provider and orders the rest, and the administrator can fix the file and restart the service. Mistakes that stop the boot (a wrong fstab entry for a needed file system, an unbootable kernel option) are handled by single-user mode and by the loader's ability to boot a different kernel, which have no counterpart on MS-DOS other than a boot floppy.

Labs#

All MS-DOS outputs below were captured on MS-DOS 4.00 built from source, booted in DOSBox-X with tools/dos_run.py (16 MB of memory, Pentium-class CPU unless stated otherwise). The lab files are in labs/08-memconfig/; .ASM and .C files and the CONFIG.SYS variants have CR LF line endings for DOS, the FreeBSD files in labs/08-memconfig/freebsd/ have LF. FreeBSD outputs are either taken from the real release files in build/freebsd/root or were captured on 2026-11-09 in the course's FreeBSD 15.1 virtual machine (Module 0: 2 GB of memory, 1 GB of swap, two virtual CPUs), and each caption says which. Your counts, times and process IDs will differ.

Lab 8.1: Map the first megabyte#

Goal. Locate every region of Figure 8.1 on a running MS-DOS 4.00 system, with MEM, DEBUG and a program that reads the BIOS data area, tests A20 and classifies the upper memory area.

What you need. The lab image, nasm, labs/08-memconfig/memmap.asm and labs/08-memconfig/BDA.TXT (a DEBUG script).

Steps.

  1. List the device drivers too: python tools/dos_run.py "MEM /DEBUG". Compare with Output 8.1.

  2. Assemble and run the mapper, and dump the BIOS data area, the start of the text screen, the video BIOS header and the top of the system ROM with DEBUG, reading commands from a file:

    Terminal
    $ nasm -f bin -o MEMMAP.COM labs/08-memconfig/memmap.asm
$ python tools/dos_run.py --file A:\MEMMAP.COM=MEMMAP.COM --file A:\BDA.TXT=labs/08-memconfig/BDA.TXT "MEMMAP" "DEBUG <BDA.TXT"

  3. Solve the 16-byte puzzle of Section 8.2: run MEM under three names of different length.

    Terminal
    $ python tools/dos_run.py --file A:\M.EXE=build/dos4/SRC/CMD/MEM/MEM.EXE --file A:\MEMORYXX.EXE=build/dos4/SRC/CMD/MEM/MEM.EXE "SET" "M" "MEM" "MEMORYXX" "CHKDSK"

What you should see. MEM /DEBUG adds the names of the resident drivers inside IO.SYS (CON, AUX, PRN, CLOCK$, A: - B:, COM1, LPT1 to LPT3, COM2 to COM4) to Output 8.1. The mapper and DEBUG:

Output 8.6 – MEMMAP.COM and DEBUG on MS-DOS 4.00 in DOSBox-X

Output 8.7 – The length of a program's name changes the free memory
---- SET
COMSPEC=A:\COMMAND.COM
PATH=A:\
---- M
    581568 largest executable program size
---- MEM
    581568 largest executable program size
---- MEMORYXX
    581552 largest executable program size
---- CHKDSK
    581552 bytes free

What is going on. The BIOS data area starts with the I/O addresses of COM1 (03F8), COM2 (02F8) and LPT1 (0378); the word at 0040:0013 is 0280h = 640, the value INT 12h returns and SYSINIT uses as the top of the arena. The video mode is 3 (80 x 25 colour text) and the CRT controller is at 3D4h, so text lives at B800:0000 as character/attribute pairs: 5A 07 is a grey-on-black Z, the first letter of DOSBox-X's own Z:\> prompt still on the screen. The A20 test writes two values at 0000:0500 and reads them back through FFFF:0510, which is linear 100500h with A20 open and 000500h with A20 closed (Example 8.1); both values came back, so A20 is closed, as expected on a system without HIMEM.SYS.

Example 8.1 – The A20 test of MEMMAP (excerpt of labs/08-memconfig/memmap.asm)
        cli
        xor     ax, ax
        mov     es, ax
        mov     ax, 0FFFFh
        mov     ds, ax                  ; DS = FFFF, ES = 0000
        mov     bx, [es:500h]           ; save the word we will change
        mov     word [es:500h], 0AA55h
        mov     cx, [510h]              ; FFFF:0510 = linear 100500h, or 000500h if A20 is off
        mov     word [es:500h], 055AAh
        mov     dx, [510h]
        mov     [es:500h], bx           ; restore

The page map is DOSBox-X's UMA, and it differs from a 1988 PC in instructive ways. In text mode the emulated VGA decodes only B8000-BFFFF, so A000-B7FF read as nothing. The video BIOS at C000 is 16 KB (size byte 20h x 512) and its bytes sum to zero modulo 256, the same test EMM386's rom_srch makes. C400-EFFF is empty: 176 KB of address space with no memory behind it, which is exactly what an EMS page frame needs. The system ROM occupies F000-FFFF; its last 16 bytes hold the reset jump (EA 5B E0 00 F0 = JMP F000:E05B), the BIOS date and the model byte FC (AT class). The equipment word 4467h comes from DOSBox-X's BIOS; decode it with Ralf Brown's Interrupt List.

The puzzle: EXEC copies the environment for the child and appends the program's full path to it (Module 3, Section 3.7). The environment here is COMSPEC=A:\COMMAND.COM, PATH=A:\ and the terminating zero, 33 bytes; then come a word and the path. With A:\MEM.EXE the block needs 46 bytes, 3 paragraphs; with A:\MEMORYXX.EXE or A:\CHKDSK.COM it needs more than 48 bytes, 4 paragraphs. The environment block is allocated before the program's own block, so a longer name leaves 16 bytes less for the program.

Questions.

  1. MEM prints the first three lines of Output 8.1 from constants. Which of the three regions did MEMMAP actually look at, and where in Output 8.6 do you see each?
  2. Change MEMMAP so that it also reports the first MCB segment (function 52h, Module 2) and the size of the largest free block (function 48h with BX = FFFFh). Why does the latter report 0 unless the program first shrinks its own block?
  3. Run MEMMAP with --file A:\CONFIG.SYS=labs/08-memconfig/cfg/C13EMM.SYS and then after EMSTEST K (Lab 8.3). Which pages change, and why are the page-frame pages "-" until a program maps something?

Lab 8.2: The price list of CONFIG.SYS#

Goal. Measure the conventional memory cost of each CONFIG.SYS keyword and explain every delta from the structure sizes in the source.

What you need. labs/08-memconfig/cfg/*.SYS (one variant per file; each differs from "no CONFIG.SYS" in one respect) and labs/08-memconfig/price.py, which boots the system once per variant with tools/dos_run.py --file A:\CONFIG.SYS=... and runs MEM /PROGRAM.

  1. Run all variants (about 15 seconds each): python labs/08-memconfig/price.py.

  2. Open build/lab08-price/C02BUF30.txt and the other raw outputs, and compare the System Data sub-blocks with NONE.txt.

  3. For the variants that load drivers, capture the drivers' own messages by running SCREEN first (Module 0): nasm -f bin -o SCREEN.COM tools/screen.asm, then for example python tools/dos_run.py --file A:\CONFIG.SYS=labs/08-memconfig/cfg/C11SMART.SYS --file A:\SCREEN.COM=SCREEN.COM "SCREEN".

What is going on. Section 8.2 explains each row. Three observations deserve a second look. The SMARTDRV row costs nothing because the driver refused to install: SCREEN shows "Microsoft SMARTDrive Disk Cache v2.10" and "SMARTDrive : No hard drives on system", the message of NO_HARDFILES (SMARTDRV.ASM lines 7540), and an uninstalled driver gets its memory back. The three RAM disks differ only in where the 64 KB live: inside the driver (0106E0 = 67,296 bytes of conventional memory), in extended memory (65,536 bytes less "available extended memory", 15,417,344 - 15,351,808, with EMM386's 304 KB already gone), and in four EMS pages under a single handle (free EMS drops from 262,144 to 196,608; RAMDRIVE.ASM lines 4558-4594). The resident code of the /E and /A drivers is 2,000 and 1,856 bytes. Every RAMDrive volume claims to have been created on 06-09-1985: the date is a constant in the driver, where CHKDSK finds it in the volume label entry.

Questions.

  1. Predict, then measure, the cost of BUFFERS=45 and of FILES=255. Show your arithmetic.

  3. A 1989 user with 512 KB of extended memory wants a 384 KB RAM disk and the largest possible conventional memory. Which RAMDRIVE switch, and why is /A with EMM386 the wrong choice on that machine?

Lab 8.3: Expanded memory with EMM386 and INT 67h#

Goal. Load the 1988 EMM386.SYS built from source, see the processor in virtual-8086 mode, allocate and map EMS pages from your own program, and test the installation checks on other processors.
