Example 8.2 – Writing through window 0, then mapping four pages at once (excerpt of labs/08-memconfig/emstest.asm)
.wr:    mov     ax, 4400h               ; map logical page BX into physical page 0
        mov     dx, [handle]
        int     67h
        mov     al, bl
        add     al, '0'
        mov     [tag_n], al
        mov     es, [frame]
        xor     di, di
        mov     si, tag
        mov     cx, tag_len
        rep     movsb
        push    cs
        pop     es
        inc     bx
        cmp     bx, 4
        jb      .wr

        xor     bx, bx                  ; 9. Map logical page i into physical page i, read all four
.map:   mov     al, bl
        mov     ah, 44h
        mov     dx, [handle]
        int     67h
        inc     bx
        cmp     bx, 4
        jb      .map

What is going on. SMSW stores the low 16 bits of CR0 and, unlike MOV EAX,CR0, is not privileged, so a V86 program can read the PE bit: with EMM386 loaded, DOS runs in protected mode. The program wrote four different strings into the same addresses, C400:0000, after mapping logical pages 0 to 3 into window 0 in turn; mapping the pages into windows 0 to 3 shows all four strings at four addresses. That is bank switching, implemented by map_EMM_page (Listing 8.11) as four page-table entries per call. The 35 mappable pages are the 24 conventional pages 4000-9C00 (handle 0, 060000 = 384 KB) and 11 pages of the UMA found empty in Lab 8.1; the page frame is C400-D3FF. With K, the handle survives the program: EMS pages are owned by handles, not by processes, and EXEC's clean-up at exit knows nothing about them (Module 2, Section 2.6). MEM /DEBUG lists the leaked handle by the name the program gave it with function 5301h; every run of EMSTEST K leaks another 64 KB until the next reboot.

With 1 MB of memory there is no extended memory (MEM prints no extended line at all, because SYSI_EXT_MEM is 0), xbuf_chk finds nothing to allocate and sets the "insufficient memory" message: the driver does not install and its memory is returned, all but 32 bytes (589,392 instead of 589,424): MEM /PROGRAM still shows an EMM386 DEVICE= entry of 10h bytes, because the driver sets its break address one paragraph above its start "to reserve the DOS link pointer" even when it refuses to install (INIT.ASM lines 289-293), and SYSINIT keeps that paragraph and its DEVMARK. On the emulated 286 and 8086 the boot hangs before the banner, for the two reasons of Section 8.3: the first conditional jump the driver executes is already a 386-only instruction, and the jump that acts on the processor test tests the wrong flag. DOSBox-X's 286 also reports 14,336 KB of extended memory where the Pentium reports 15,360 KB with the same 16 MB, and its 8086 none; that is the emulator's choice, not DOS's.

Questions.

  1. _MapHandlePage reloads CR3 before map_page writes the new entries (Listing 8.10). Why is that still correct here? Describe a change to the code after which it would not be.
  2. Why must functions 43h and 45h be reflected to V86 mode while 44h is handled in ring 0? (Hint: who runs int67_Entry, and what does allocation touch?)
  3. With FILES=20, BUFFERS=20 and DEVICE=\EMM386.SYS (the lab image's CONFIG.SYS with ANSI.SYS replaced by EMM386.SYS), MEM reports 548,576 bytes. Predict that number from Output 8.1 and Lab 8.2 before you run it.

Lab 8.4: The C heap on MS-DOS#

Goal. See how much a Microsoft C 5.10 program can malloc in the small and the large memory model, and relate every number to DOS's arena.

What you need. labs/08-memconfig/heap.c and tools/dos_tools.py.

Example 8.3 – Allocating until malloc fails (excerpt of labs/08-memconfig/heap.c; dos_free asks DOS for FFFFh paragraphs and prints the largest free block)
    while ((p = malloc(CHUNK)) != NULL) {   /* malloc is _nmalloc in small, _fmalloc in large model */
        p[0] = 1;
        if (first == NULL)
            first = p;
        n++;
    }
    printf("malloc(%d) succeeded %u times: %lu bytes; first block at %Fp\n",
           CHUNK, n, (unsigned long)n * CHUNK, (char far *)first);
    dos_free("after malloc:");

    while ((fp = _fmalloc(CHUNK)) != NULL) {  /* the far heap: more segments from DOS */
        fp[0] = 1;
        nf++;
    }
    printf("then _fmalloc(%d) succeeded %u times: %lu bytes\n", CHUNK, nf, (unsigned long)nf * CHUNK);

Steps.

  1. Copy heap.c to a work directory as HEAP.C, build both models and the link map of the small one:

    Terminal
    $ python tools/dos_tools.py --dir work "CL /AS /FeHEAPS.EXE HEAP.C" "CL /AL /FeHEAPL.EXE HEAP.C" "CL /AS /Fm /FeHEAPS.EXE HEAP.C"
$ python tools/dos_run.py --file A:\HEAPS.EXE=work/HEAPS.EXE --file A:\HEAPL.EXE=work/HEAPL.EXE "MEM" "HEAPS" "HEAPL"

  2. Read the segment table at the top of work/HEAPS.MAP and the EXE header fields e_minalloc and e_maxalloc (offsets 0Ah and 0Ch of the file; a few lines of Python with struct.unpack will do).

What you should see. MEM reports 581,568 bytes, then Output 8.4. The link map and the headers:

Output 8.12 – The segments of HEAPS.EXE (LINK map) and the allocation fields of both EXE headers
 Start  Stop   Length Name                   Class
 00000H 01A11H 01A12H _TEXT                  CODE
⋮
 01EC0H 024BFH 00600H c_common               BSS
 024C0H 02CBFH 00800H STACK                  STACK

 Origin   Group
 01A2:0   DGROUP

HEAPS e_minalloc=0x00e3 e_maxalloc=0xffff
HEAPL e_minalloc=0x009b e_maxalloc=0xffff

What is going on. Section 8.5 explains the three results. DGROUP starts at paragraph 01A2h of the image (6,688 bytes of code before it); 256 + 6,688 + 65,536 = 72,480 is exactly the difference between MEM's 581,568 and the 509,072 free at start, minus the 16-byte MCB. The near heap is what is left of DGROUP after the data, the BSS and the 2 KB stack: _memavl() reports 60,716 bytes, and 59 blocks of 1,024 bytes (plus a 2-byte header each) fit. first block at 13B6:12D2 is a near pointer printed with DGROUP's segment: 1204h (PSP) + 10h + 1A2h = 13B6h. In the large model, the first block is at 23F1:000C, in a segment that the library got from DOS above the program, and malloc ends when both DOS and the near heap are empty.

Questions.

  1. Why does the small-model malloc fail with 509,072 bytes still free in DOS? What would a programmer of 1988 do to use them, and what does that cost in the source code?
  2. Link HEAPS.EXE with /CP:1 (LINK's /CPARMAXALLOC), so that e_maxalloc asks for the minimum. Does the free memory at start change? Explain with Module 2's description of EXEC.
  3. free() all the far blocks and call dos_free again. Does DOS get the memory back? Compare with jemalloc's dirty_decay_ms in Section 8.5.

Lab 8.5: The rc system by hand#

Goal. Read FreeBSD's default configuration, order a set of real rc.d scripts with the rcorder algorithm by hand, check the result with a model of rcorder, and write an rc.d script for a small daemon.

What you need. The release files in build/freebsd/root/etc, a POSIX shell with grep (on Windows: Git Bash), Python, and labs/08-memconfig/rcorder.py, labs/08-memconfig/freebsd/heartbeat and labs/08-memconfig/freebsd/heartbeat.rc. The last steps need the FreeBSD virtual machine.

Steps.

  1. Find some defaults, and the headers of eleven scripts:

    Shell
    cd build/freebsd/root/etc
grep -nE '^(rc_conf_files|early_late_divider|syslogd_enable|sshd_enable|cron_enable|dumpdev)=' defaults/rc.conf
cd rc.d
grep -E '^# (PROVIDE|REQUIRE|BEFORE|KEYWORD):' dumpon swap fsck root mountcritlocal FILESYSTEMS syslogd DAEMON LOGIN sshd cron

  2. On paper, using only these eleven files: draw one node per script and an arrow from each provider of a required condition to the script that requires it (and from a BEFORE: script to the providers of the condition). List the conditions that nobody provides. Give every script its sequence number as do_file does (Listing 8.25), and write down the lines that rcorder -p would print.

  3. Check your answer with the model, then run it on all 171 scripts, skipping nostart as /etc/rc does, and ask it why sshd comes so late:

    Shell
    d=build/freebsd/root/etc/rc.d
python labs/08-memconfig/rcorder.py $d/dumpon $d/swap $d/fsck $d/root $d/mountcritlocal \
    $d/FILESYSTEMS $d/syslogd $d/DAEMON $d/LOGIN $d/sshd $d/cron
python labs/08-memconfig/rcorder.py --dir $d -s nostart
python labs/08-memconfig/rcorder.py --dir $d --why sshd

  4. Read heartbeat (the daemon) and heartbeat.rc (its rc.d script, Example 8.4), and check the shell syntax of both, here and again in the VM with FreeBSD's /bin/sh: sh -n labs/08-memconfig/freebsd/heartbeat and sh -n labs/08-memconfig/freebsd/heartbeat.rc.

  5. In the VM, as root, in the directory where you copied the two files: install and start the service, then exercise rc.subr:

    Shell
    install -m 755 heartbeat /usr/local/libexec/heartbeat
install -m 755 heartbeat.rc /usr/local/etc/rc.d/heartbeat
service heartbeat start          # refused: heartbeat_enable is NO
sysrc heartbeat_enable=YES heartbeat_interval=2
service heartbeat start; sleep 5
service heartbeat status; service heartbeat last
procstat -c $(cat /var/run/heartbeat.pid)
service heartbeat stop; tail -2 /var/log/heartbeat.log
rcorder /etc/rc.d/* /usr/local/etc/rc.d/* | grep -n -e heartbeat -e '/LOGIN$'
service -e | grep heartbeat

  6. Still in the VM, check the model of step 3 against the real rcorder: the subset, the full set (with line numbers, which are the sequence numbers), and the example of rcorder(8):

    Shell
    cd /etc/rc.d
rcorder -p dumpon swap fsck root mountcritlocal FILESYSTEMS syslogd DAEMON LOGIN sshd cron 2>&1; echo $?
rcorder -p -s nostart * | awk '{ print NR ": " $0 }'
rcorder -k nostart -s firstboot -s nojailvnet * | wc -l

    When you no longer need the service (Exercise 8.1 uses it again), remove it with sysrc -x heartbeat_enable heartbeat_interval and rm /usr/local/etc/rc.d/heartbeat /usr/local/libexec/heartbeat /var/log/heartbeat.log.

Example 8.4 – An rc.d script for a toy daemon (labs/08-memconfig/freebsd/heartbeat.rc)
#!/bin/sh
#
# PROVIDE: heartbeat
# REQUIRE: DAEMON
# KEYWORD: shutdown
#
# Lab 8.5: an rc.d script for the toy daemon /usr/local/libexec/heartbeat.
# Install as /usr/local/etc/rc.d/heartbeat (mode 755) and enable it with
#   sysrc heartbeat_enable=YES
# Optional settings in /etc/rc.conf (defaults below):
#   heartbeat_interval="10"                 seconds between two lines
#   heartbeat_log="/var/log/heartbeat.log"  where the lines go

. /etc/rc.subr

name="heartbeat"
desc="Toy daemon that writes a line every few seconds"
rcvar="heartbeat_enable"

load_rc_config $name

: ${heartbeat_enable:="NO"}
: ${heartbeat_interval:="10"}
: ${heartbeat_log:="/var/log/heartbeat.log"}

pidfile="/var/run/${name}.pid"
procname="/usr/local/libexec/heartbeat"
command_interpreter="/bin/sh"
command="/usr/sbin/daemon"
command_args="-f -p ${pidfile} -o ${heartbeat_log} ${procname} ${heartbeat_interval}"

extra_commands="last"
last_cmd="${name}_last"

heartbeat_last()
{
	tail -n 3 "${heartbeat_log}"
}

run_rc_command "$1"

41: rtadvd rwho ubthidhci local lpd mountlate hcsecd nscd ntpd bootparams powerd rarpd apm sdpd msconvd moused utx ftp-proxy
42: bthidd swaplate mountd nuageinit_user_data_script rfcomm_pppd_server
43: LOGIN nfsd
44: syscons sshd cron sendmail inetd sysctl_lastload msgs
45: bgfsck jail
46: securelevel
# rcorder -k nostart -s firstboot -s nojailvnet * | wc -l
       3

The first start is refused by run_rc_command, which tests heartbeat_enable with checkyesno before it starts anything (rc.subr lines 1331-1343). While the service runs, ps -ax | grep heartbeat shows the two processes that daemon(8) creates: the supervisor, which renames itself daemon: /usr/local/libexec/heartbeat[13684] (daemon), and its child 13684, the shell running the script, whose pid is the one in the -p file. heartbeat requires only DAEMON (sequence 40), so it gets sequence 41 and rcorder prints it before LOGIN (43), among the other scripts of sequence 41.

What is going on. The subset shows how rcorder treats conditions without providers: it warns, sets its exit status to 1, and orders the rest anyway; that is why /etc/rc sends rcorder's errors to /dev/null (Listing 8.24). DAEMON lands at sequence 1 in the subset because NETWORKING and SERVERS have no providers there; on the full set it is at 40. The full ordering also explains the two passes: everything up to FILESYSTEMS (sequence 15) runs in the first pass, before /usr/local/etc/rc.d is searched. The chain to sshd is a longest path: sshd itself requires only LOGIN and FILESYSTEMS, but LOGIN depends, through DAEMON, SERVERS and NETWORKING, on nearly everything else. The model's per-line sets match what rcorder 15.1 computes (Listing 8.25): in the course VM the 46 lines of rcorder -p -s nostart contain exactly the 46 sets of Output 8.14, only the order inside a line differs (it is left to qsort), and both count the 3 scripts of the rcorder(8) example (bluetooth, power_profile, wpa_supplicant). The subset taught one more detail: rcorder warns about a BEFORE: on an unknown condition only when no file mentions that condition at all. add_require enters every required condition in the table even if nobody provides it, and insert_before warns only for a new entry (rcorder.c lines 288-302, lines 599-606), so dumpon's BEFORE: disks is silent because swap requires disks; only cron's securelevel is reported. In heartbeat.rc, load_rc_config runs before the : ${...:=...} defaults, so values from rc.conf win; command is daemon(8), which detaches, writes the child's pid to the -p file and the output to -o; procname and command_interpreter tell check_pidfile that the process to look for is /bin/sh running the script (Section 8.7). The daemon starts sleep in the background and waits for it, because sh defers a trapped signal until a foreground command finishes, and wait is interrupted at once.

Questions.

  1. Add # BEFORE: LOGIN to heartbeat.rc. Which sequence number does it get now, and which does LOGIN get? Check with the model (copy the script into a directory with the release's scripts) and with rcorder -p in the VM.
  2. What happens at boot if a script says # REQUIRE: nosuchthing? And if two scripts require each other? Answer from satisfy_req and do_file (Section 8.7), then test with the model and, in the VM, with rcorder.
  3. Why does heartbeat.rc use procname and command_interpreter instead of letting run_rc_command look for a process named daemon?

Lab 8.6: Watching FreeBSD memory#

Goal. Read FreeBSD's memory counters, relate them to the page queues, and watch a process's virtual and resident size while it allocates and touches memory.

What you need. The FreeBSD VM (2 GB of memory and 1 GB of swap in Module 0's setup) and labs/08-memconfig/freebsd/touchmem.c. Everything in this lab runs in the VM; the outputs below were captured in the course VM, and the static facts they rely on (sysctl names, top's sources, jemalloc's configuration) are in Sections 8.4 and 8.5. No step uses more than 256 MB, so the lab is safe on a shared machine.

Steps.

  1. The machine:

    Shell
    sysctl hw.physmem hw.realmem hw.usermem hw.pagesize
sysctl vm.stats.vm.v_page_count vm.stats.vm.v_free_count vm.stats.vm.v_active_count \
       vm.stats.vm.v_inactive_count vm.stats.vm.v_laundry_count vm.stats.vm.v_wire_count
swapinfo -h; sysctl vm.swap_total vm.swap_reserved vm.overcommit
vmstat 1 5
top -b -o res 10

  2. Build and run the program in one terminal while vmstat 1 runs in another:

    Shell
    cc -O0 -o touchmem touchmem.c
./touchmem 256
MALLOC_CONF=dirty_decay_ms:0,muzzy_decay_ms:0 ./touchmem 256
MALLOC_CONF=stats_print:true ./touchmem 16 2> stats.txt
grep -E 'Version|opt\.(retain|oversize_threshold|dirty_decay_ms|muzzy_decay_ms):|^Merged|^arenas\[|^decaying|^ +dirty:' stats.txt
truss -o touchmem.truss ./touchmem 16 > /dev/null
grep -c '^break' touchmem.truss; grep -E '^(mmap|madvise)' touchmem.truss | tail -3
Example 8.5 – The touching loop (excerpt of labs/08-memconfig/freebsd/touchmem.c)
	for (i = 1; i <= 4; i++) {
		for (off = (i - 1) * step; off < i * step; off += page)
			p[off] = 1;		/* first write to a page: a page fault */
		printf("touched %zu MB\n", i * step >> 20);
		show("after touching");
		sleep(2);
	}

hw.pagesize and vm.stats.vm.v_page_size are both 4096. hw.realmem is exactly the 2 GB that Hyper-V gives the VM, hw.physmem is 38 MB less, and hw.usermem is hw.physmem minus the wired pages, to the byte: 2,107,146,240 - 93,381 x 4,096 = 1,724,657,664. v_page_count x 4,096 = 2,060,668,928, another 44 MB below hw.physmem. The five counts, however, add up to 510,603 pages, 7,510 more than v_page_count: the counters are not a partition of memory taken at one instant. vm_page_wire counts a managed page as wired at once but only flags it for a deferred dequeue (PGA_DEQUEUE), so the page stays in its queue's count until a batched queue operation or the page daemon processes the flag (vm_page.c lines 4228-4232, vm_pageout.c lines 1485-1492). top's "Mem:" line shows the same counts converted to KB and printed with a K or M suffix (Listing 8.17): 263M Inact is 67,251 x 4 KB, 365M Wired is 93,381 x 4 KB; "Buf" is vfs.bufspace, not a page queue. vm.overcommit is 0, and 368 MB of swap are reserved although none is used. In vmstat, fre is the free count (1.3G), but avm (4.0T) is not user memory: vmtotal() adds up the size of every active VM object in the system (vm_meter.c lines 220-253), and the kernel's own kernel_object alone is as large as the kernel's address range (vm_object.c lines 279-280), while no process in top is larger than 25 MB. vmstat prints these short forms only on a terminal; piped or redirected it prints plain bytes, because it sets hflag = isatty(1) (vmstat.c line 216).

The allocation behaves as Section 8.5 predicts: after malloc RSS grows by 104 KB, while VSZ grows by 329,728 KB (322 MB). That is more than 256 MB, and truss shows why on the 16 MB run: jemalloc rounds a large request plus one page (16 MB + 4 KB) up to its next size class and maps a 20 MB extent, plus a 2 MB block aligned to 2 MB (MAP_ALIGNED(21)) for its metadata; VSZ grows by 22,528 KB = 22 MB. For 256 MB the same pair is 320 MB + 2 MB. In some runs VSZ grows by 337,920 KB instead; in such runs truss shows a third, 8 MB MAP_ALIGNED(21) block. Each touching step adds 65,664 KB of RSS: 64 MB of data plus 128 KB for the 32 page-table pages that map it (one per 2 MB), which count as resident memory of the process (pmap.c lines 1599-1609). vmstat shows 17k page faults (flt) in the same second, 16,384 of them for the 64 MB, while fre falls from 1.3G to 1.1G over the four steps. truss shows no break call at all.

What happens at free contradicts a natural expectation. RSS falls by only 512 KB and VSZ not at all, also 12 seconds later, and setting both decay times to 0 changes nothing. The statistics explain it: the 16 MB block, like the 256 MB one, is above opt.oversize_threshold (8 MiB) and was served by the extra arena arenas[8] (nine arenas for opt.narenas 8), whose dirty decay time is 0, while arenas[0] keeps the 10-second default (Section 8.5). So free purged the block at once in both runs: one madvise of 4,097 pages, the madvise(..., 16781312, MADV_FREE) at the end of the truss output, and no munmap. MADV_FREE leaves the pages mapped and resident until the page daemon needs memory (Section 8.5), and opt.retain keeps the address range, so VSZ stays too. Only at exit does everything go: the last vmstat row shows 77k pages freed (fr) and fre back at 1.3G. Note also opt.muzzy_decay_ms: 0: jemalloc 5.3.0's source makes 0 the default (arena_types.h lines 6-8), although jemalloc(3) still says "The default decay time is 10 seconds" (jemalloc.3 line 959). The version string is the one in jemalloc.h line 102.

What is going on. malloc(256 MB) only creates a mapping (Module 2, Section 2.5); the pages exist when a fault first touches them, which is when RSS and the page counts change. Steps 1 and 2 together are the FreeBSD version of Lab 8.1: on MS-DOS, MEM could account for every byte from the arena; here the accounting is by page state, and "free" memory is low on a busy system because the page cache keeps file pages in the active and inactive queues. Two details of touchmem itself are worth copying. It runs ps with two -o options, because ps(1) takes the text after = as the column header, "a string that spans the rest of the argument": -o vsz=,rss= prints a single column headed ",rss=". And it gives ps an empty MALLOC_CONF; otherwise ps inherits stats_print:true and prints its own statistics at every call.

Questions.

  1. Overcommit and the OOM killer, safely. (a) Run limits -v 256m ./touchmem 512. Which call fails, and which kernel check refuses it? (b) Copy touchmem to a directory that an ordinary user can read (/tmp/t), run sysctl vm.overcommit=1; su -m nobody -c '/tmp/t/touchmem 2048'; sysctl vm.overcommit=0, and read dmesg. Relate the result to Listing 8.18. Why must you not repeat (b) as root? © The system-wide experiment, ./touchmem 4096 with vm.overcommit=0, fills RAM and swap until the OOM killer of Listing 8.19 kills a process. Do it only in a VM of your own, from a snapshot, and never on a shared machine: it was not run in the course VM. Predict from Listing 8.19 and vm.pageout_oom_seq what happens and what dmesg would say.
  2. In top -o res, which processes are largest after boot? Which of them are started by rc.d scripts you met in Lab 8.5?
  3. ps reports RSS for touchmem but MS-DOS's MEM reports block sizes. Which DOS number corresponds to VSZ, which to RSS, and why is the distinction meaningless on MS-DOS?

sysctl -d prints the descriptions compiled into the kernel; the one for vm.overcommit is the string next to Listing 8.18 (swap_pager.c lines 179-181). sysctl -aT lists kern.maxfiles and vm.pageout_oom_seq (both CTLFLAG_RWTUN) but neither vm.overcommit (CTLFLAG_RW) nor hw.physmem (a TUNABLE_ULONG_FETCH in hammer_time() and a read-only sysctl). The -a matters: a bare sysctl -T has nothing to filter and prints only its usage message (Section 8.8). Setting kern.maxfiles works at once; setting hw.physmem fails because the OID is read-only. service -e lists the enabled scripts in rcorder order, heartbeat among them. In the course VM sshd is already enabled (the course tools log in with SSH), so sysrc -c sshd_enable=YES returns 0 and sysrc -c sshd_enable=NO returns 1: -c only checks, and "for assignments, return success if no changes are required, otherwise failure" (sysrc(8)). On a fresh installation without sshd the two results are reversed.

What is going on. KEYB with a layout went resident: 5,792 bytes (575,776 instead of 581,568), and KEYB US later switched the layout inside the resident copy without giving any memory back. KEYB's environment block, freed when it went resident, now holds MEM's environment (011FF0, just below KEYB). MODE changed the serial port and the keyboard repeat rate through the BIOS and exited; it costs nothing. On FreeBSD, the flags in Listing 8.27 decide which variables can change: a variable that the kernel reads only once at boot (hw.physmem) cannot be changed later, because the decisions made with it (here, the size of the page arrays) cannot be undone, the same reason that BUFFERS= needs a reboot on MS-DOS.

Questions.

  1. Load KEYB twice with different layouts. What does the second call do to memory? Find the answer in KEYBCMD.ASM (look for the code that detects an installed copy) and confirm it with MEM.
  2. Which FreeBSD sysctl corresponds most closely to FILES=, and why can it be changed at run time when FILES= cannot?
  3. Give one FreeBSD setting from each of the four classes of Section 8.8 that you would change on a server with 2 GB of memory and no swap, and say where you would write it.

Study cases#

Study case 8.A: Getting more than 640 KB#

Goal. Compare three answers to "the program needs more memory than the address space gives it": bank switching on a board, EMM386's emulation of that board with paging, and FreeBSD's virtual memory.

The problem. In 1985 a spreadsheet on an 8088 had 640 KB minus DOS, and 20-bit addresses. More memory could only be added outside the address space, so the program had to see it through a window. LIM EMS made that window explicit: four 16 KB windows, a function to change what each shows, and handles that name the pages (Figure 8.2). The program, not the system, decides which data is visible at each moment; a pointer into a window is valid only while the right page is mapped; and a data structure larger than 64 KB has to be cut into pages by hand.

The 386 answer inside MS-DOS. The 386 had paging, and EMM386 uses it to emulate the board (Section 8.3). The application interface stays exactly the same: the 386 does in four page-table entries what the board did in a register. map_EMM_page (Listing 8.11) and FreeBSD's pmap_enter (pmap.c lines 7104-7106) do the same job, writing page-table entries for a virtual address, but they are called for opposite reasons: map_EMM_page because a program asked for a different window, pmap_enter because the kernel decided, during a page fault (vm_fault, vm_fault.c line 1686), that a page should now be there. EMM386 is a virtual machine monitor whose only virtual-memory feature is a faithful copy of a hardware limitation; the comment in Listing 8.6 even promises to emulate the 64 KB limit "faithfully".

The FreeBSD answer. Each process has its own address space, and the kernel maps any page anywhere on demand. The program sees one flat memory; which physical pages back it, and whether they are in RAM or in swap, is the kernel's business.

EMS board (LIM 3.2/4.0) EMM386 FreeBSD 15.1
Visible at once 64 KB (4 windows) 64 KB, plus mappable conventional pages the whole address space
Unit 16 KB page 16 KB = 4 x 4 KB 386 pages 4 KB page (2 MB superpages)
Who maps the program, INT 67h 44h the program; the monitor writes PTEs the kernel, at fault time
Pointers valid only while mapped same always valid
Protection none none between programs per page, per process
On exit handles stay allocated (Lab 8.3 leak) same address space destroyed
Cost of a mapping change I/O port writes two traps to ring 0 and a reflection, 4 PTE writes, CR3 reload page fault, pmap_enter, TLB shootdown
Running out function 43h fails same overcommit, then the OOM killer

What to notice. The EMS interface survived for years after hardware that could do better was common, because the programs were written against it; EMM386 is the cost of that compatibility (37 KB of conventional memory, a privileged monitor, DMA and A20 emulation). FreeBSD's VM is the same hardware feature used for the opposite purpose: to hide the memory layout from the program instead of exposing it.

Discussion questions.

  1. An EMS 4.0 multitasker (DESQview, for example) used the mappable conventional pages to give every program its own copy of the memory above 256 KB. Which FreeBSD mechanism does that resemble, and what is missing?
  2. Why does a DMA transfer need special care under EMM386 but not under FreeBSD's busdma framework, which also deals with physical addresses? (Hint: who knows that the buffer is paged?)
  3. Lab 8.3's handle leak cannot happen to FreeBSD processes. Can a FreeBSD process leak memory that outlives it at all? Think of System V shared memory and tmpfs.

Study case 8.B: From CONFIG.SYS to rc.d#

Goal. Compare what "configuring the system" means on each, using one task: start a resident service at boot, with a setting, and later change the setting.

MS-DOS. Add INSTALL=\KEYB.COM IT,,\KEYBOARD.SYS to CONFIG.SYS (or a KEYB line to AUTOEXEC.BAT) and reboot. The order is the order of SYSINIT's passes and of the lines; the setting is a command-line argument; the cost is 5,856 bytes of conventional memory (Lab 8.2); to change the layout, edit the file and reboot, or type KEYB US and live with the resident copy. Nothing records that KEYB is "a service"; MEM shows a block named KEYB.

FreeBSD. Install a script in /usr/local/etc/rc.d that declares what it needs (REQUIRE: DAEMON), set heartbeat_enable=YES and heartbeat_interval=2 with sysrc (two lines in /etc/rc.conf), and run service heartbeat start. At boot, rcorder computes the position from the declarations of all 171 base scripts and the local ones (Lab 8.5); the setting lives in rc.conf and overrides a default in the script; changing it means sysrc and service heartbeat restart, with no reboot. service -e lists the service as enabled.

What to notice. Three things are separated on FreeBSD that are one on MS-DOS: data (defaults files plus small overrides), code (one script per service, sharing rc.subr), and order (declared dependencies instead of positions). The separation is what makes mistakes local: a wrong value in rc.conf affects one service and produces a warning (checkyesno), a missing dependency produces a warning and an order (rcorder), and the administrator can repair the system while it runs. On MS-DOS a configuration line is executed by the code that builds the kernel's tables; a mistake can cost one line ("Error in CONFIG.SYS line n"), the whole boot (SHELL=), or, with a misbehaving driver, the stability of everything that follows. On the other hand, the MS-DOS system is completely described by two short files that a user can read in a minute; FreeBSD's equivalent is 795 lines of defaults, 171 scripts and a 2,800-line library.

Discussion questions.

  1. rcorder orders by declared dependencies; SYSINIT by passes and position. Give a situation in which the MS-DOS approach is safer.
  2. CONFIG.SYS cannot be changed while the system runs, and neither can a FreeBSD RDTUN tunable. Is the reason the same?
  3. Where would you put the FreeBSD equivalent of "load ANSI.SYS before anything else that writes to the screen", and what would you declare?

Homework#

Hand in source files, transcripts of the runs, and answers as one archive. Cite source lines with permalinks as these notes do; mark FreeBSD outputs as captured in your VM.

Exercise 8.1: Configure two machines#

Difficulty: intermediate. Estimated time: 3 h.

A small office in 1989 has a 386 with 2 MB (640 KB + 1,408 KB extended) and one hard disk; the same office in 2026 has a FreeBSD server with 2 GB of memory and no swap. Requirements: Italian keyboard and date format, 40 open files, a 512 KB RAM disk for temporary files, a disk cache, an EMS page frame for a spreadsheet, as much conventional memory as possible; on FreeBSD: sshd and cron running, a 512 MB memory-backed /tmp, the open-files limit raised to 200,000, overcommit refused when swap reservation fails, and the "heartbeat" service of Lab 8.5.

Tasks:

  1. Write CONFIG.SYS and AUTOEXEC.BAT for the 1989 machine. Boot them on the lab image with tools/dos_run.py (the lab machine has no hard disk: explain which lines therefore do nothing, and why) and report MEM /PROGRAM. Compute the conventional memory cost of each line from Section 8.2 and compare with the measurement.
  2. Write /boot/loader.conf, /etc/rc.conf and /etc/sysctl.conf for the 2026 server. For each line, say whether it takes effect at boot, at run time or at the next service start (Section 8.8), and cite the source or man page that supports the claim. Apply them in your VM and show sysctl and service -e.

Deliverables: the five files, two transcripts, and a two-column table mapping each requirement to the lines that implement it on each system.

Hints: EMM386 takes its pool size in KB (Section 8.3); RAMDRIVE and SMARTDRV take /E or /A; tmpmfs and tmpsize are in /etc/defaults/rc.conf; vm.overcommit is described in tuning(7).

Exercise 8.2: MEMINFO, a memory report for MS-DOS#

Difficulty: intermediate. Estimated time: 3 h.

Write MEMINFO.COM (nasm) that reports: conventional memory (INT 12h), the largest free block (function 48h with BX = FFFFh), extended memory (INT 15h function 88h, and 0 if the carry flag is set), and free and total expanded memory (INT 67h function 42h, only if an EMMXXXX0 driver is present). Print sizes in KB or bytes. Optionally write the same program in Microsoft C 5.10 with int86 and intdos (dos.h).

Run it on the lab image without CONFIG.SYS, with cfg/C13EMM.SYS, and with --conf-extra cpu.cputype=286 and --conf-extra dosbox.memsize=1. Explain every difference with MEM's output for the same configurations.

Deliverables: source, the four transcripts, a paragraph per difference.

Hints: a .COM program owns the largest block when it starts; what will function 48h find unless you first shrink your own block with function 4Ah? MEM.C (lines 640-870) does all four measurements.

Exercise 8.3: An rc.d script for a memory watcher#

Difficulty: intermediate. Estimated time: 3 h.

Write a FreeBSD service memwatch: a shell script daemon that appends a line with the time and vm.stats.vm.v_free_count, v_inactive_count and v_laundry_count to a log every memwatch_interval seconds, and an rc.d script for it that follows the conventions of Lab 8.5. Requirements: memwatch_enable, memwatch_interval (default 10), memwatch_log; a start_precmd that refuses to start when the interval is not a positive integer; an extra command report that prints the minimum free count in the log; settings read from /etc/rc.conf.d/memwatch; REQUIRE chosen so that the log directory is mounted.

Deliverables: both scripts; sh -n output; a VM transcript of start, status, report, stop, a start with an invalid interval, and rcorder output showing the script's position.

Hints: rc.subr calls ${name}_precmd-style functions through start_precmd; returning non-zero from it cancels the start. Use daemon(8) as heartbeat.rc does, and test the daemon itself in a terminal first.

Exercise 8.4: The processor check that could not work#

Difficulty: advanced. Estimated time: 4 h.

  1. Write CPUTYPE.COM (nasm, cpu 8086) that identifies an 8086/8088, a 286 and a 386 or later with the flag test of Is386 (Listing 8.12), prints the model byte at F000:FFFE, and then executes EMM386's own sequence (or ax,ax / jz / call Is386 / jnz) to report which branch it takes. Run it with --conf-extra cpu.cputype=8086, 286, 386 and pentium.
  2. With ndisasm, find the bytes of Is386 and of its caller in build/dos4/SRC/MEMM/MEMM/EMM386.SYS (Output 8.3 shows how), and explain why the original driver hangs on a 286 before it calls Is386.
  3. Fix the source so that a 286 gets "EMM386 not installed - incorrect machine type." Rebuild EMM386.SYS from a copy of build/dos4/SRC/MEMM with tools/dos_tools.py ("CD MEMM\MEMM" "NMAKE"), install it with --file A:\EMM386.SYS=..., and test it on the 286 and the Pentium. List every instruction you had to change and why.

Deliverables: CPUTYPE.ASM, transcripts, the patch (a diff of the changed .ASM files), and a one-page explanation.

Hints: in MASM 5.10, jz short label forces the 2-byte form. Follow the path that a 286 takes through Init_MEMM386 up to the printing of the message and the return to SYSINIT, not just the first jump.

Exercise 8.5: Overcommit in practice#

Difficulty: intermediate. Estimated time: 3 h.

In the FreeBSD VM, write overcommit.c, which allocates memory in 64 MB steps with malloc (or with mmap(MAP_ANON), chosen by an option), optionally touches every page, and prints after each step the values of vm.swap_reserved, vm.swap_total (read with sysctlbyname(3)) and its own RSS. Run it with vm.overcommit set to 0 and to 1, with and without touching, with and without a swap file (mdconfig and swapon, see swapinfo(8)). For each run, report where it stopped (which call failed, or which signal killed it, and the kernel message in dmesg), and explain it with Listings 8.18 and 8.19.

Deliverables: source, a table of runs, explanations with permalinks.

Hints: do the runs that touch memory without a limit only on a snapshot of a VM of your own, never on a shared machine; the OOM killer may choose a process other than yours. limits -v 512m ./overcommit ... makes any run safe and shows a third way to fail. Run the vm.overcommit=1 cases as an ordinary user (root is never refused, Listing 8.18) and put the old value back afterwards. Read RSS from kinfo_proc (sysctl(3) with KERN_PROC_PID): getrusage(2)'s ru_maxrss is a peak sampled at clock ticks and lags behind.

Exercise 8.6: Essay: memory scarcity as a design driver#

Difficulty: basic. Estimated time: 2 h.

Write 1,200 to 1,500 words on how the scarcity of memory shaped MS-DOS 4.00's configuration and memory management, and how abundance shaped FreeBSD's. Use at least four concrete examples from this module with measured numbers (for instance: the paragraph rounding of every CONFIG.SYS table, EMM386 shipping its tables above 1 MB, kern.maxfiles computed from the memory size, jemalloc's decay timers). Discuss one place where FreeBSD still economises on memory, and one place where MS-DOS spent memory generously.

Further reading#

  • Lotus, Intel and Microsoft, Lotus/Intel/Microsoft Expanded Memory Specification, version 4.0, 1987: the INT 67h interface that Section 8.1 and Lab 8.3 use.
  • Ray Duncan (ed.), The MS-DOS Encyclopedia, Microsoft Press, 1988: chapters on memory management, device drivers and CONFIG.SYS.
  • Ralf Brown's Interrupt List: INT 12h, INT 15h functions 87h and 88h, INT 67h, and the BIOS data area.
  • Intel, 80386 Programmer's Reference Manual, 1986: chapters on paging and virtual-8086 mode.
  • Marshall Kirk McKusick, George V. Neville-Neil and Robert N. M. Watson, The Design and Implementation of the FreeBSD Operating System, 2nd ed., Addison-Wesley, 2014: chapter 6, memory management.
  • The FreeBSD Handbook, chapters "The FreeBSD Booting Process" and "Configuration, Services, Logging and Power Management": docs.freebsd.org/en/books/handbook/.
  • Manual pages of the release: rc.conf(5), rc(8), rc.subr(8), rcorder(8), loader.conf(5), sysctl(8), tuning(7), malloc(3), daemon(8), service(8), sysrc(8).
  • Jason Evans, "A Scalable Concurrent malloc(3) Implementation for FreeBSD", BSDCan 2006: the origin of jemalloc.
